chapters.title: A Haunting from the Past
paragraphs: Magnamainak

Fifteen years have passed since we gained independence. According to the ancient laws of India, our Goddess of Liberty has now come of age; the time has come to cast aside our escapist tendencies and face the hard truth. Therefore, this story may now be told.

I begin this tale with a precocious youth named Nengti Dutta, for had it not been for him, we would never have become involved in this affair. It was Nengti who, almost by force, made his way into our home and struck up an acquaintance with Byomkesh. He was an exceedingly self-assured boy, quick of tongue and sharp of wit, perhaps seventeen or eighteen years old, though his thin and wiry frame made him appear even younger. At this age, he had already acquired considerable intelligence, yet there was a touch of childish foolishness about him as well—a curious blend of boyishness and premature cunning. At first acquaintance, he seemed rather cheeky and impudent, but we soon discovered he was not ill-natured at heart. He harbored a deep, secret admiration for Byomkesh, though from his manner of speaking, one might think he had seen through all of Byomkesh’s cleverness and fancied himself the more astute of the two.

Whenever he visited our house, he would engage Byomkesh in discussions on criminology, speaking with the air of a seasoned expert. He had long since abandoned formal studies, but was by no means ignorant. Byomkesh, amused, would indulge him with a smile. Despite the difference in their ages, a bond of affectionate banter soon developed between them.
After a few days of coming and going, Nengti suddenly reached out his hand one day and said, “Byomkesh-babu, give me a cigarette, won’t you?”
Byomkesh stared at him in astonishment, then rebuked him, “You’re just a boy, and you smoke cigarettes?”

Nengti replied, “Where would I get them to smoke? My aunt never gives me a single paisa, and now and then I steal one or two from my uncle’s tin. Besides, is it even possible to smoke at home? The moment my aunt smells smoke, she comes charging at me. Come on, give me one.”
Byomkesh handed him a cigarette, which he smoked with great care, then departed, promising to return soon.
Thereafter, whenever he visited, we had to give him a cigarette.
One day, Nengti arrived in a state of great excitement and said, “You know, Byomkesh-da, a girl has come to our house—she looks just like an English mem!”
Byomkesh, entirely unperturbed, replied, “Is that so?”
Nengti said, “Yes, I’ve never seen such a beautiful girl in my life. If you saw her, you’d be left cross-eyed.”
Byomkesh said, “In that case, I’d better not see her. Who is she?”

Nengti said, “She’s my uncle’s friend’s daughter. Used to live in East Bengal. Her parents were killed in the Hindu-Muslim riots; the girl barely escaped with her life. My uncle gave her shelter, let her stay in the house. Her situation is much like mine.”

Inwardly, I offered my respects to Nengti’s uncle, Santosh Samaddar. Though I had never met him in person, I knew of him through Nengti. He was a renowned figure; his political and business exploits were well known throughout Bangladesh. We were also familiar with his family circumstances. In fact, the story I am about to recount is a family affair of Santosh Babu himself.

What I learned about the members of this family, both before and after the incident, I shall record here in brief. It was a sudden death that brought us into contact with this prosperous household. And again, it was a sudden death that drew the final curtain on the last act of this drama. I haven’t seen Nengti in many days—but let that be.

Santosh Samaddar was a wealthy businessman, closely involved in the independence movement in the political sphere. A little way south from Chowringhee, on a side street, stood his sprawling two-storied, garden-surrounded house. Yet Santosh Babu was seldom at home; he spent his days absorbed in business matters and political meetings, returning only after dusk. Even then, on Saturday evenings he was never to be found at home; after finishing his office work, he would go to the house of a kirtan singer to listen to music, and from there, on Monday mornings, he would head straight to the office. At that time, he was about forty-eight years old.

His wife, Chameli Samaddar, was two or three years younger than he. A tall, slender, nervous woman, she had been involved with the revolutionaries in her youth. After marrying Santosh Babu, she spent several years quietly fulfilling her domestic duties and had given birth to twin sons. Gradually, however, she developed obsessive tendencies; her nature grew sharp and fault-finding. Fish and meat disappeared from the household, and apart from sharing the same roof, all other relations with her husband ceased. Thus passed the last ten or twelve years.

Their twin sons were Jugalchand and Udaychand. Twenty years old, both attended college. Though twins, the brothers were utterly different in appearance and character; Jugalchand was slim and delicate-featured, while Udaychand was burly and rough-hewn. Jugalchand was calm by temperament, good at his studies, secretly wrote poetry. Uday was arrogant and unruly, quarreled with everyone, and, defying his mother’s wishes, would go to hotels to eat chicken. Sreemati Chameli could not control him, but perhaps, in her heart, she loved him a little more than his brother.

Besides these four, three others lived in the house. First, Nengti and her younger sister Chingri. Two years ago, their parents had died together of cholera, leaving Nengti and Chingri orphans. Sreemati Chameli was not their actual maternal aunt, but she had brought them into her home; they had been there ever since. I have already introduced Nengti; Chingri was three or four years younger. She was petite, but on the whole, pretty; even at her age, she had become clever and adept at household work. Owing to her aunt’s obsession with cleanliness, she spent most of her time in the scullery—Chingri ran the household. Jugalchand had nicknamed her “Kucho Chingri”—tiny shrimp.

The third person living in the house was Rabibarma. His full name was probably Rabindranath Barman, but he was better known as Rabibarma. Tall and skeletal in build; the shape of his face, the slant of his eyes, and the scantiness of his moustache and beard marked him as a native of the Tripura region.
Byomkesh Samagra

I had my suspicions; he appeared to be around forty. He was one of Santosh Babu’s employees, the secretary responsible for all his political activities. Having no family of his own, he lived in Santosh Babu’s house, had become one of the household; when necessary, he even looked after the domestic affairs.

Into this circle of seven, the day an exquisitely beautiful young woman arrived, none saw the sly smile that flickered across the face of the god of death. Nengti had been the first to bring word of the young woman’s arrival; since then, every time he visited, he was absorbed in discussing her, describing the powerful currents of attraction and repulsion that had begun to surge within the family. Listening to him, I felt as though a calamity was gathering over Nengti’s household, but I never imagined it would take such a deadly form.

It was about six months after the young woman’s arrival. Durga Puja was over, and preparations for Kali Puja had begun. One evening, after dusk, Byomkesh sat in our baithak-khana, reading the Ramayana under the lamplight, utterly absorbed. Rajshekhar Basu Mahashoy had trimmed and polished the original Valmiki Ramayana, making it crisp and lucid; Byomkesh, in those saltless hours of idle days, was trying to devour it with his help. I lay sprawled on the takhtposh, lost in lazy, scattered thoughts. From the few pieces I’d read in the recent Sharadiya magazines, it seemed to me that Bengali writers had forgotten how to write Bengali; just as we have gained independence in the realm of the nation, so too in language—unfettered, ungoverned autocracy... The human mind today is running wild, brazenly trespassing on land, water, and sky... This morning I saw in the newspaper that a plane from Chattogram to Calcutta had crashed into the sea... a Pakistan Airlines plane—not a single soul survived, a long list of the dead has been published... We have become skyfarers, our feet no longer touch the earth... Poet Satyen Dutta wrote about airplanes, ‘udgat-pakha jādrel pipīlikā’—‘a fierce-winged ant’—a most striking metaphor.
“Do you know the name of Parvati’s brother?”
I sat up on the takhtposh. Byomkesh had set aside the Ramayana and was lighting a cigarette. I said, “Parvati’s brother? Which Parvati?”
Byomkesh exhaled smoke and said, “Mahadev’s Parvati, Parvati the daughter of the Himalayas.”
“Oh, I see. Did Parvati have a brother?”

“She did.” Byomkesh raised his forefinger and began to speak in a lecturing tone, “His name was Mainak Parvat. In those days, mountains had wings, they would fly about, settling wherever they pleased atop cities and settlements. You can imagine the state of those cities and settlements. Seeing this, Indra, king of the gods, grew angry, took up his thunderbolt. Wherever there were mountains on earth, he burned off all their wings with his thunder. Only Himalaya’s son Mainak escaped; he fled to Setubandh Rameshwar and hid beneath the sea. Since then, Mainak lies under the ocean, sometimes poking out his nose, then diving back down. Rather like a fugitive criminal.”
I asked, “Indra was such a great god, yet he couldn’t catch Mainak?”
Byomkesh replied, “Indra was indeed king of the gods, but he was not a satyanweshi. Besides, he was a notorious drunkard and libertine.”

I was pondering how, despite being a notorious drunkard and libertine, Indra became king of the gods, when suddenly, from the next room, the telephone rang out with a bright, tinkling sound. It had been ages since I’d heard such a sweet noise; my heart instantly leapt with excitement. Surely, someone was in trouble—
MAGNA MOINA K
Byomkesh had been sought out for refuge. Before Byomkesh could rise from his chair, I leapt forward and picked up the telephone. It would not be right to keep a desperate supplicant waiting.

Hearing Nengti’s voice on the line, I was momentarily taken aback; but after listening to her message, I felt invigorated once more. Nengti said, “Ajit-babu, please bring Byomkesh-da quickly. Hena Mallik is dead.”
Hena Mallik—the exquisitely beautiful young woman. Excited, I exclaimed, “Dead? What happened?”
Nengti replied, “She fell from the roof on the third floor and died. The police have arrived. Mesomoshai isn’t home—it’s Saturday—please come at once.”
Byomkesh came over and took the telephone from my hand. “Who is this, Nengti? What’s happened?”
He listened for a while, then said, “Alright—we’ll see—” and hung up.

We returned to the baithak-khana. The clock showed it was seven thirty-five. Byomkesh, brows furrowed, began to pace the room. I watched him for a moment and then asked, “Are you wondering whether to go?”
He said, “I’m wondering whether we ought to go. The master of the house hasn’t called us; perhaps it’s nothing but an accident. In that case, is it proper to go just because Nengti has summoned us?”

I considered and said, “The master isn’t home. The others are just youngsters. The police have arrived. Perhaps Nengti’s aunt asked her to send word to us. If we go as family friends in this situation, would it be so wrong?”
Byomkesh frowned a little longer, then said, “That’s true. Come, let’s go.”

We reached Santosh-babu’s house around half past eight. No one was at the gatehouse. The house itself was barely visible in the darkness; only on the outer wall, I noticed a bamboo scaffolding tied up. Perhaps repairs and whitewashing were underway before Dewali.

Upon entering, we found ourselves in a large, well-appointed hall. Four or five powerful electric bulbs overhead lit the room as bright as day. In the center stood a low, round table, surrounded by several chairs and sofas. As we entered, we saw eight or ten men present, most of them in police uniform.

No one noticed our arrival. An inspector sat at the table, bent over, writing something in a diary, while the others stood around him, all eyes fixed on the inspector. Excluding the police, only four others were present; among them, I recognized Nengti. Of the remaining three, one was obviously the secretary, Ravi Verma—his Mongolian features made that clear. The other two were young men, so they must be Yugalchand and Udaychand. Both had the stunned, limp look of those still numb from shock, the true reaction yet to set in.

We stood by the doorway. Byomkesh cast his gaze once around the room. On the left, there was no furniture, only a telephone atop a tall side table in the far corner; in the center, several men gathered around the round table; to the right, near the wall, a white sheet-covered form lay on the floor—a body. Beyond that, on the lowest step of the staircase leading to the upper floor, two women sat pressed close together—surely Sreemati Chameli and Chingri. Their eyes were filled with unmitigated terror; they did not look at the shrouded corpse, but stared fixedly at the group of people in the middle of the room.
Byomkesh, too, took in everything at a glance and moved forward in that direction, coming to stand before the table.
Byomkesh suddenly exclaimed, “Aré! Who is this?”

The Inspector looked up from his diary; the others turned their heads to see. Closing his diary, the Inspector came forward to stand before Byomkesh, extending his hand as he said, “Byomkesh! Where have you come from?”

Byomkesh shook his hand, but did not answer the question; instead, he introduced me. I learned that his name was Atulkṛiṣṇa Ray, known in short as A. K. Ray. He had been Byomkesh’s classmate in college, now stationed in Calcutta. Though I had not met him before, he and Byomkesh saw each other from time to time. Later I would come to know, he was a jovial man, but during work he was grave and sparing of words.
Byomkesh asked, “What’s the matter? I heard a girl has died?”
“Yes.” After a moment’s thoughtful silence, A. K. Ray said, “Come, I’ll tell you.”

We stepped a little away from the group, and A. K. Ray recounted the incident in brief. He was now the officer-in-charge of the local thana. At ten minutes to seven this evening, he received a telephone call reporting an accidental death at Santosh Babu’s house; the call had come from the secretary, Ravi Verma. A. K. Ray had arrived at once with his men. On the western side of the house, where the fence had not yet been built, right near the foundation, the body of a young woman had been found. A. K. Ray had brought the police doctor along; after examination, the doctor declared that the cause of death was a broken neck from a fall from a height, the time of death estimated at about an hour before, that is, around six-thirty. A. K. Ray then went up to the open terrace on the third floor and found, in the middle of the roof, a small mat laid out, beside it a pair of feminine slippers. On inquiry, he learned that the girl would come up to the terrace every day at sunset and sit there. There was no doubt she had gone up today as well, and had fallen from the terrace to her death.
Finishing his account, A. K. Ray asked again, “But who informed you?”
Byomkesh pointed towards Nengti and said, “That boy. His name is Nengti Dutta. He comes to see me from time to time. I suppose he panicked and called me.”
Nengti was standing a little distance away, looking in our direction. A. K. Ray observed him intently for a moment and said, “Hmm. So, what do you want to do now?”
Byomkesh replied, “What can I do? I’ve come merely as a family friend, not as a satyanweshi. What do you think? Accidental death?”
A. K. Ray said, “It appears to be an accident. However—” He left the sentence unfinished, a hint of a smile flickering in his eyes.
Byomkesh nodded. “Have you taken everyone’s statements?”
A. K. Ray replied, “Yes! Only the master of the house is yet to be found. No one seems to know where he is. I hear he’s never home on weekends.” Again, that smile glimmered in his eyes.
Byomkesh said, “When you’ve prepared copies of the statements, will you give me one?”
A. K. Ray replied, “Certainly. You’ll have it by tomorrow afternoon. Do you want to see the body?”
Byomkesh said, “I can have a look. Why not?”
A. K. Ray led us to where the shrouded corpse lay, lifted the edge of the sheet and drew it aside. In the harsh, brilliant light, I saw the dead Hena Mallik.
She had indeed been beautiful, Nengti had not lied. Her complexion was like milk tinged with alta, her hair thick and jet black—

Disheveled as she was, it only seemed to lend her face a more intimate charm, as if her brows had been painted with a delicate brush. Her eyes were half-closed, the deep blue irises barely visible, her body brimming with the bold exuberance of youth. Death had stolen only her soul, leaving not a single mark upon her body, unable to rob even a fraction of her youthful beauty. The thought that this body would, within two days, be reduced to ashes was almost unbearable.

We gazed, spellbound, when suddenly a sound behind us made us turn our heads. Jugal and Uday had come to stand behind us. Uday’s eyes were bloodshot, both fists clenched. He turned to Jugal and roared, “Jugal, you killed Hena.”
Jugal lifted his fiery eyes to Uday and replied in a thin, hard voice, “I—killed Hena! Liar! You killed her.”

Had there been a moment’s delay, I believe a silent, deadly battle would have erupted between the two brothers. But the two women sitting on the stairs did not allow it. Sreemati Chameli and Chingri rushed forward together and stood between them. Chameli, pressing her hands against Uday’s chest, pushed him back, her sharp, broken voice ringing out, “Wretched boy! What are you saying? Go away from here, go to your own room. No one killed Hena, she fell from the roof and died herself.”
Meanwhile, Chingri clutched Jugal’s hand and pleaded in a hurried, anxious tone, “Dada, I beg you, come away, don’t stay here. Come to your bedroom—please!”
The quarrel was quelled, but neither of the two left the room; with bloodshot eyes, they continued to glare at each other.

Neither Byomkesh nor the police made any attempt to intervene in this sudden outburst. They stood by, entirely detached, watching. From their demeanor, it seemed they were waiting to see if, in the heat of the quarrel, some hidden truth might be revealed. But when the fight broke off midway, the inspector went to Uday and asked, “Just now you accused your brother of killing Hena. Is there any basis for this accusation?”

Uday did not answer, remaining stubbornly silent. Sreemati Chameli shot a piercing glance at the inspector, but before he could say anything, the atmosphere in the room seemed to change as if by magic.

A middle-aged gentleman had appeared at the main door. Of medium height, somewhat heavyset but not fat; his face lacked softness, but there was a firmness to it. His attire was a touch elegant—a collared panjabi and a pleated dhuti, beneath which peeked white leather Vidyasagari slippers. I had seen his photograph countless times in the newspapers; thus, I had no trouble recognizing Santosh Samaddar. Yet what I had never gleaned from those pictures I now sensed: the man possessed a powerful presence. Wherever he was, he was the center; no one else could command attention.
At the sight of him, Sreemati Chameli made no comment, but hurried up the stairs. A moment later, Uday too went upstairs. The rest of us remained as we were.

When I saw Santosh Babu, he was standing by the door, his unwavering gaze fixed on the body lying on the floor. Without looking at anyone, he walked over to the dead woman’s feet. As he stared, the muscles in his face grew taut, his eyes clouded with mist, then cleared again. Without addressing anyone, he spoke slowly, “So, father, mother, daughter—all lost to untimely deaths! What a strange fate.”

No one had expected that he would be overwhelmed with grief at the death of his dependent friend’s daughter, yet I was not prepared for this unyielding composure either; it struck me as a little too dry and hard. Nevertheless, he lifted his gaze from the corpse and turned his eyes to each of us in turn.
Byomkesh, a bit awkwardly, cleared his throat and said, “You might call us uninvited guests. My name is Byomkesh Bakshi, and this is my friend Ajit Bandyopadhyay. You do not know us, but Nengti—”
Santoshbabu said, “I do not know you, but I know your names. Did Nengti bring you here?” He turned his eyes to Nengti.
Nengti, who had been standing behind, replied in a nervous voice, “I—Masima was very frightened—”

“You did well to inform Byomkeshbabu. In times of trouble, one always thinks of a friend first.” There was a hint of warmth in his tone as he turned to Byomkesh and said, “Nengti is your friend, I suppose?”
Byomkesh replied, “You could say so.”
Santoshbabu said, “Very good, very good.” Then, turning to A. K. Ray, he asked, “Is your work done?”
A. K. Ray replied, “All our work is finished; as soon as the body is dispatched, we’ll be leaving.”

Perhaps the thought had not occurred to Santoshbabu; he paused and said, “That’s right. There must be a post-mortem.” He glanced briefly at the corpse and said, “I have nothing to say. Do what you must.”
He started towards the stairs, but A. K. Ray called after him, “If you don’t mind, I’d like to ask you a few questions.”
Santoshbabu stopped and said, “Why should I mind? Please, be seated. I’ll be back in a moment. Robi, show them to the dining room. And Chingri, arrange for tea and refreshments for them.”
He went upstairs. Robi Varma came forward and said, “Please come with me.”
A. K. Ray stationed an officer by the body and followed Robi Varma; we went along with him.

Santoshbabu’s dining room was quite large; a long table could seat twelve or fourteen people at once. We took our seats on the chairs. I noticed that Jugalchand, Nengti, and Chingri had not come with us. Robi Varma did not sit down; he remained standing by the door, awaiting his master’s return.
Byomkesh had taken the chair next to A. K. Ray and asked, “Have you seen Hena Mallik’s room?”
A. K. Ray replied, “I’ve seen it, more or less. Just a very ordinary bedroom. Not much furniture either.”
Byomkesh asked, “Any letters or papers?”
A. K. Ray replied, “I haven’t had a proper look yet. I’ll check again before I leave. Would you like to see it?”
“I would.”
At that moment, the officer who had been guarding the body came over and whispered into A. K. Ray’s ear—
Magamaenak Pantry, kitchen, servants’ quarters Telephone Hall Staircase Dining room Bathroom Corpse Ravi Varma Rohan

In a low voice, he said, “The van has arrived, shall we send the body off?” A. K. Ray replied, “Go ahead.” The officer left. We sat in silence. Ravi Varma stood by the open door, gazing unblinking toward the hall. Through his eyes, it was as if we ourselves witnessed the removal of the corpse. For a fleeting moment, a hungry, unsated longing flickered in his Mongolian eyes, only to vanish at once. That brief glance revealed that Secretary Ravi Varma’s feelings toward Hena were not entirely devoid of attachment.

Afterwards, Santosh Babu entered and seated himself at the head of the table. He had shed his elegant attire for plain, everyday clothes. Sitting down, he said, “Ravi, bring some cigarettes.” Ravi Varma hurried off to fetch them. Santosh Babu looked at A. K. Ray and said, “Perhaps you wish to ask me about Hena? Regrettably, I don’t know much about her. I did give the girl shelter, but never really had the chance to know her well. For one, I’m rarely at home, and besides, Hena was not a particularly sociable girl. In any case—” Ravi Varma returned with a tin of cigarettes and a box of matches, placing them before Santosh Babu. He opened the tin and offered it to us. “Please.” As Byomkesh reached for a cigarette, he smiled slightly and said, “I’d heard smoking was forbidden in this house.” Santosh Babu frowned ever so slightly and replied, “Not for you gentlemen.” He took a cigarette himself, struck a match, and extended it toward us. “Now, ask whatever questions you wish.”
Byomkesh Samagra
A.K. Ray signaled to the writer-jamadar, who produced a notebook and pencil. The questioning then began.

Question: What is Hena’s father’s name? Answer: Kamal Mallik. Question: Was Kamal Mallik your friend? Answer: Yes. I had known him for nearly fifteen years. Because of my business, I have had to travel all over India, and I still do. I first met Kamal Mallik in Dhaka, and gradually we became close. Question: So you saw Hena even before she came to Calcutta? Answer: Many times. I have known her since she was three or four years old. Question: Did taking her in create any disturbance in your household? Santoshbabu paused for a moment, then said, “My wife was displeased. She is a stickler for cleanliness; Hena is a girl from Pakistan, she has no sense of propriety—using that as an excuse, my wife refused to let Hena eat from our kitchen. There’s a hotel nearby, so I arranged for Hena’s meals to be brought from there.” Question: No one else objected? Answer: No one else would dare object. Question: Did Hena have any interaction with anyone in the house? Answer: There was no restriction on interaction. But Hena was not a sociable girl, and perhaps she had not yet recovered from the shock of her parents’ deaths. So she kept to herself, rarely leaving her room. Question: Did you know she used to go up to the terrace on the third floor every evening? Answer: I didn’t know before; I learned of it today. Question: From whom did you learn this? Answer: From the person who telephoned me with the news of her death. Question: Who informed you of her death? Santoshbabu rested his hand on his cheek for a moment, then looked up and said, “That’s just it—I didn’t notice who it was. No one even knows the address of where I was staying.” Suddenly, he turned a sharp gaze toward Robi Verma and said, “Robi.” Robi Verma replied in a deep voice, “No, sir, I didn’t make the call.” We exchanged glances. A.K. Ray asked, “Didn’t you recognize the voice on the telephone?” Santoshbabu said, “After receiving the news, no other question even occurred to me. But—” A.K. Ray now asked the inevitable question, “Where were you?” A faint flush crept into Santoshbabu’s face. He looked at each of us in turn and said, “Is it absolutely necessary to know that?” A.K. Ray seemed a little uncomfortable; it was evident from his demeanor. He said awkwardly, “Forgive me, but I am still not entirely certain about the circumstances of Hena Mallik’s death. It is quite possible that she accidentally fell from the terrace, but we cannot entirely rule out the possibility that someone pushed her. That is why we need to know everything.” Santoshbabu raised his brows and looked at A.K. Ray for a while, then said, “Hena—”
MAGNA MOINA K 763

“Is it possible that someone pushed him?” A.K. Ray replied, “Yes, it is.” Santosh Babu raised his voice slightly, “But who would kill him? And why?” A.K. Ray shook his head, “That I do not know yet. But we must investigate every possibility.” Santosh Babu sat for a while, his hand on his cheek, then suddenly straightened up; surveying us all with a stern gaze, he said in a hard tone, “Very well, let me tell you where I was. But this is a secret of my life—let there be no talk about it.” “There will be no talk. Whatever you say will remain off the record.” A.K. Ray gestured to the other police officers; they rose and went into the hall, and the writer-jamadar closed his notebook and left as well. Byomkesh made as if to rise, saying, “Then perhaps we too should go to the next room.” Santosh Babu raised his hand and said firmly, “No, you stay. In fact, it is good that you are here—I now appoint you to safeguard my family’s interests.” Byomkesh sat down again. Santosh Babu lit another cigarette and drew on it gently, while we waited in silence. From near the prawn door, Chingri craned his neck and asked, “Shall I bring in the tea?” Santosh Babu said, “Yes, bring it.” Chingri entered the room, followed by two servants carrying trays of food and tea. As Chingri set the cups and plates before us, he cast a wide-eyed glance at Byomkesh. He must have heard of Byomkesh from Nengti. In his gaze there was not only curiosity, but something else—something harder to define. Perhaps, inwardly, he was afraid. Santosh Babu said, “Serve those outside as well.” Chingri left with the servants for the hall, and Ravi Varma quietly closed the door behind them. We turned our attention to the refreshments. Santosh Babu took only a single cup of tea, and after a tentative sip, began to speak without looking at us: “I am not a man of spotless character, but for that I blame no one but myself. Among my many flaws, one is that I am fond of listening to kirtan.” We looked up at him. In politics, Santosh Babu was a renowned orator; there was no doubt that he would relate his secret with a moving gravity. Indeed, the variety of his preamble drew our undivided attention. After another sip of tea, he took a long drag on his cigarette, then, dropping the burnt stub into the cup and pushing it aside, he began: “You may have heard of the kirtan-singer Sukumari. Singing is her profession—she performs at gatherings for money. Ten years ago, I heard her sing and was enchanted. My married life was not happy, and I became attracted to Sukumari. She was then twenty-two or twenty-three. For some time, I visited her house in secret, and we became close. But all sorts of people came to her house—some to listen, some to book her for performances. I realized it was not safe for me to keep going there. “You know that my life is closely entwined with politics. In the struggle for independence—”
Byomkesh Samagra

I have fought, I have gone to jail, I have been beaten by police batons, I have given countless sums to revolutionaries, and during the Partition, I have acted as a messenger between both sides. In the realm of politics, I have a reputation, I have influence. And naturally, I have enemies as well. If my adversaries ever get the chance to spread scandal in my name, my fame and position will be ruined. After much deliberation, I took a certain step: I rented a small house under an assumed name. My intention was to take Sukumari there, to end her public life as a singer. But Sukumari would not agree to this. In the end, it was decided that she would remain in her own home and continue her music business, but twice a week—on Saturdays and Sundays—she would come and stay at my rented secret house. I would come and go in such a way that no one would know.

For the past ten years, this arrangement has continued. On Saturday afternoons, after finishing my office work, I go there, and then on Monday morning, I go straight from there to the office. That is what happened today as well; around half-past three, I arrived there. Then—at eight in the evening, I received a telephone call and left immediately.' A dry sarcasm flickered across his face. 'That is my alibi.'

Digesting the sting of his irony, A.K.R. said in a gentle tone, 'Thank you. Pardon my impertinence, but if I may ask just a couple more questions, I will release you. Is there any servant or attendant at the rented house?'

Santoshbabu replied, 'No, I have deliberately kept no servant. Every Saturday at noon, Sukumari comes from her own house to the rented one and tidies up the rooms. I arrive in the afternoon. Then, after I leave for the office on Monday, she locks up and returns to her own home. The house remains closed for the rest of the week.'
Question: Why have you kept a telephone there?
Answer: Not for myself, but for Sukumari. When she is at the rented house, she wants to keep in touch with her own home. But it is a private number; you will not find it in the directory.
Question: Did you tell the number to your secretary?
Answer: No.
Question: Is it possible that anyone else knows?
Answer: No one could possibly know. I have told no one, and Sukumari will not tell anyone either.
Question: Do you trust her?
Answer: I do. I give her a thousand rupees a month. She is no fool; she would not cut off her own feet.
Question: When you received the telephone call today, what were you doing?
Answer: I was listening to kirtan. Sukumari was singing the verses of Chandidas.

A.K.R. turned his eyes to Byomkesh; Byomkesh shook his head silently, meaning, there were no further questions. Then A.K.R. rose and said, 'That will be all for today. Forgive us for troubling you. Will you be—going back again tonight?'
'No, I will not return; I shall stay at home.' A glint of amusement played in Santoshbabu’s grave eyes as he said, 'You will not find my house by setting a spy after me.'

A.K.R. clicked his tongue and said, 'No, no, nothing of the sort! I have not the slightest curiosity about your secret residence. What you have told us is sufficient for our investigation. Only—if we could meet Srimati Sukumari once, that would be helpful.'
'You will find her at her own address.' Santoshbabu handed over Sukumari’s address and stood up. 'It is ten o’clock. Your work is probably not yet finished; stay as long as you need.'
M G MOINAK

chapters.title: A Death in the Samaddar House
paragraphs: “Certainly,” Byomkesh replied, rising to his feet.
Santosh-babu said, “Well then, I’ll go and take some rest. I’m feeling a bit fatigued.”

He strode out of the room with firm steps. There was no sign of weariness in his body. Perhaps it was fatigue of the mind. After such a calamity in the house—Santosh-babu had revealed his secrets with neither evasion nor subterfuge, made no effort to justify himself. When one must speak the profound truths of life, it is best to speak plainly. Yet, his ruthless honesty could not help but trouble me. He was a seasoned businessman and a shrewd politician; perhaps his character would have been better without that dark stain.
A.K. Ray asked Byomkesh, “And now?”
Byomkesh said, “Come, let’s take a look at Hena’s room.”
“Let’s go. Shall we go up to the roof as well?”
“We shall. Since we’re here, let’s see all that needs to be seen.”

Near the round table in the hall, the remaining police officers were conversing in low voices. Except for Ravi Verma, none of the household members were present. Hena’s room lay diagonally across from the dining room, at the far end of the hall. [See plan.] The door to Hena’s room was slightly ajar, a light burning within. The three of us entered. Ravi Verma followed close behind.

The room was quite large. On the main road side, a large arched window; on the east wall, another ordinary window. In front of this window stood a table and chair, beside them a bookshelf. On the other side of the room, a narrow, simple cot was made up; beneath it, two large suitcases were visible. In the corner of the north wall, a narrow door led to an adjoining bathroom. The room was free of clutter, and so appeared rather neat. Perhaps Hena herself was of a tidy disposition.
Standing in the center of the room, Byomkesh looked around and asked, “Was the door open?”
A.K. Ray replied, “No, it was locked. In the deceased’s hand was a leather handbag, and inside it we found a key ring. Here it is.” He produced a bunch of keys from his pocket.
Taking the keys in hand, Byomkesh said, “So Hena locked her room before going up to the roof.”
A.K. Ray said, “That’s how it appears.”

Ravi Verma made a sound like a cough, his fist before his mouth. When Byomkesh turned to him, he said, “Hena never stepped out of her room without locking the door. Never left it open, not even for a moment.”
Byomkesh asked, “Is that so? Was it always this way, or did something prompt it?”
“Always this way.”
Byomkesh said nothing further. Examining the key ring, he said, “I see there are five keys. One must be for the door lock. And the others?”
A.K. Ray replied, “Two of the others are for the suitcases. The remaining two—we haven’t identified what they open.”
Byomkesh examined each key in turn and said, “One of them has a number engraved on it—”
Byomkesh Samagra

remains—number 7. See if this key fits anywhere.” A.K.R. examined the key and said, “No. Of the two locks whose keys are missing, this is one.” “There aren’t any padlocks on the table drawers?” “There are. But all the drawers are open. The keys are missing.” “Hm. What do you think?” The two men exchanged glances for a moment. Finally, A.K.R. said, “Hard to say. Often the lock goes missing, but the key remains on the ring.” Byomkesh looked at Rabivarma and asked, “Can you say anything?” Rabivarma shook his head. “I know nothing about this room. This is the first time I’ve entered it.” Byomkesh made a sound in his throat, handed the bunch of keys back to A.K.R., and went to stand before the table.

On one side stood a table with drawers, covered in red baize, with nothing atop it but a couple of books. Then his eyes fell upon a single red rose lying on the red baize. There was no vase in the room, and the rose had been left there so carelessly, it seemed strange. Byomkesh did not touch the flower. He leaned forward to examine it closely, then raised his eyes to the open window at the head of the table and said, “Fresh flower. Are there roses in the garden?” The view beyond the window was lost in darkness. Rabivarma replied, “Yes.” Byomkesh turned to A.K.R. and asked, “What do you think about the rose? Why is it lying on the table like this?” A.K.R. silently pointed outside the window. Byomkesh nodded in agreement. “That’s what I think too. When Hena was not in the room, someone plucked the rose from the garden and tossed it onto the table through the bars of the window.” All our eyes turned to Rabivarma, the same question in each gaze—who could have thrown it? But Rabivarma avoided our questioning eyes, glancing here and there, and finally said, “I don’t know anything.” Byomkesh sighed and began opening the drawers one by one. I went to stand before the bookshelf.

Two rows of books. In the first row: Rabindranath’s *Sanchayita*, Satyen Dutta’s *Kabyasanchayan*, Nazrul’s *Sanchita*, and a few novels by modern writers. The second row held many cheap editions of English novels. Hena read foreign mysteries and thrillers too. “Ajit, look.” I turned to see Byomkesh had taken a photograph from a drawer and was staring at it intently. Mounted on cardboard, postcard-sized—a portrait of a woman. I glanced at it and exclaimed, “Hena’s photo.” Byomkesh shook his head. “No. The photo is several years old, see how yellowed it is, yet the woman can’t be less than twenty-five. It can’t be Hena, perhaps Hena’s mother. Now I see where Hena got her beauty.” I had never seen Hena alive; I had guessed her beauty from her corpse. Now, looking at this photo, it felt as though I was seeing her in life. Not just beauty—an inexhaustible vitality.
A strange radiance seemed to emanate from every corner.
Byomkesh handed the photograph to A. K. Ray and said, “Keep this. We’ll have to ask Santosh Babu whether this is a picture of Hena’s mother.”
A. K. Ray took the photograph, running his eyes over it, while Rabibarma craned his neck to get a look. The man’s face betrayed nothing, but there was a keen curiosity burning within him.
A. K. Ray slipped the photo into his pocket and asked, “Did you find anything else in the drawer?”
“No. Just a few coins—nothing of note. Rabibabu, do you know if Hena ever received any letters?”
Rabibarma replied, “I’m not at home when the post arrives. Nengti or Chingri might know.”

Without another word, Byomkesh approached the bookshelf. He glanced over the spines, then took down the volume of Sanchayita. As soon as he opened the cover, a piece of pink paper, folded neatly, came into view. Four lines of handwriting adorned the page. Byomkesh held the slip between two fingers, examining it, while Rabibarma, like a crane, stretched his neck to see.

But Byomkesh did not let him read the note; he swiftly slipped the paper into his pocket. Rabibarma’s expression did not change, but it was clear that his soul was restless with longing to read those words.

Byomkesh began opening the other books one by one, while A. K. Ray and I stood on either side, watching his every move. Since he could not see what we were doing behind him, Rabibarma grew increasingly agitated with curiosity. What was the source of such intense interest?
Nothing else was found among the Bengali books on the upper shelf. On the first page of each, in a neat, feminine hand, was written—Hena Mallik.

There were no papers in the English books on the lower shelf either, but Byomkesh drew our attention to one detail. On the title pages of several books, a rubber stamp bore the name of a bookseller from Dhaka. A. K. Ray raised his brows at Byomkesh, and I did the same. But Byomkesh said nothing; perhaps Rabibarma’s presence restrained him.
When the inspection of the books was done, Byomkesh said, “Let’s see what’s in the suitcases. Open them, will you?”

A. K. Ray took out a bunch of keys and unlocked both suitcases. Inside, various types of women’s clothing were neatly arranged in layers. Saris, skirts, ghagras, dupattas, kameezes, pyjamas—garments of every kind. All of them expensive. Byomkesh sifted through them, turning them over, then sighed and said, “No, nothing useful here. You’ve checked the bathroom, haven’t you?”
A. K. Ray replied, “Yes. Nothing noteworthy.”
“I’ll take a look myself.” Byomkesh entered the bathroom. Two or three minutes later, he returned and said, “Come, let’s go up to the roof.”

A few steps from the door, the staircase began—a broad, elegant flight of stairs. Byomkesh turned on the bottom step and said, “Rabibabu, you needn’t come with us. We can inspect the roof ourselves.” There was such firmness in his tone that Rabibarma did not protest, remaining at the foot of the stairs. We ascended.

The staircase, brushing past the first floor, wound its way up to the second. As we rounded the bend, I took in the second floor at a glance. Above the hall below was another hall, identical in every respect, and at the front corners, two rooms. The only difference was that, unlike the ground floor, there were no doors on the back wall; instead, on the second floor, three doors stood in a row. In other words, above the kitchen, pantry, and such below, were several bedrooms, their doors opening into the upper hall.

At the top of the stairs, on the third floor, stood a closed door. A.K. Ray slid back the latch and opened it, then pressed a switch by the doorway, flooding the roof with light. Under the glare of the floodlights, the vast expanse of the terrace was revealed.

The three of us stepped onto the roof. Byomkesh immediately examined the door and remarked, “I see the door can be locked from both sides—there’s a latch inside, a chain outside. A.K. Ray, when you came up to the roof, was the door closed?”
A.K. Ray replied, “No, it was open from both sides.”
The electric lights blazed, and by now, the waning moon of the dark fortnight had risen above the horizon. We walked to the center of the terrace.

The roof was enormous—one could easily lay out a fine tennis court up here. Around the edge ran a solid parapet, and along its top, bamboo poles jutted up from outside, except on the eastern side, where the scaffolding was missing—perhaps repairs had just been completed there. Beyond the roof, some twenty or twenty-five feet away at the edge of the garden, a row of tall silver pines stood at regular intervals, encircling the house like silent sentinels. From the terrace, their upper branches looked like the spires of a temple.

Byomkesh slowly turned his head, taking in the entire scene, then let his gaze return to the terrace itself. There was nothing else on the roof, save for a mat, laid a little to the west of center, and beside it, a pair of women’s rubber slippers.
A picture floated before my mind’s eye: Hena had come up to the terrace, spread out the mat, slipped off her slippers, and sat down. And then—?
Byomkesh approached this mute tableau and stood before it, gazing at it for a while. Then he raised his head and asked, “Where did Hena fall?”
Pointing toward the side where the scaffolding was missing, A.K. Ray replied, “This way.”

The three of us walked to the edge of the eastern parapet. The moon hung before us. Twenty-five feet away, the row of pines whispered in the gentle breeze, as if murmuring in low voices about Hena’s untimely death. If only they could speak the language of men, perhaps we would have the testimony of eyewitnesses. “She fell right there!” A.K. Ray pointed downward.

We leaned over and looked. In the shadow of the pines, nothing was clearly visible. The parapet reached up to my waist and was a foot wide. Hena was certainly shorter than I; even if she had leaned over for some reason, it seemed unlikely she would have toppled over the parapet.
Byomkesh, too, was silently taking measurements in his mind. He turned to A.K. Ray and said, “Hmm. The parapet is about four feet high. How tall was Hena?”
A.K. Ray, reading Byomkesh’s thoughts, replied, “About five feet three inches. But even so, it’s not impossible.”

“I didn’t say it was impossible.” Byomkesh slowly walked along the edge of the parapet. The stars had built a ladder from the ground to the roof; a sturdy man could easily climb up here using the scaffolding.
MAGNA MOINA K 769
After finishing his inspection of the roof, Byomkesh said in a slightly disappointed tone, “It’s quite late. Let’s leave it at this for tonight. —Should we seal Hena’s room?”
A.K. Ray replied, “I don’t see any need to seal it. Hena didn’t die in that room. Besides, both of us have already searched it thoroughly.”
Byomkesh said nothing more. A.K. Ray switched off the light and started down the stairs; we followed behind him.
We descended in silence. As we reached the first floor and were about to turn the corner, a muffled, sharp voice reached our ears from the side—“You will keep quiet, you will not say a word.”

I turned my head sharply and saw, at the far end of the hall on the first floor, Rabivarma and Mrs. Chameli standing face to face. Rabivarma, noticing us, seemed to silently signal Mrs. Chameli, who turned to look in our direction. Then, her eyes flashing with sharp, intolerant annoyance, she strode quickly into a room at the back.
Once downstairs, Byomkesh cast a sidelong, sardonic glance at A.K. Ray and said, “Did you hear that?”
A.K. Ray nodded slightly and said, “Come, let me drop you both home in the police van.”

The next morning, Sunday, at seven o’clock, Byomkesh and I had just sat down with our cups of tea when Nengti burst into the room with a clatter and exclaimed, “Byomkesh-da, something terrible has happened!”
Byomkesh raised an eyebrow and said, “Something terrible?”
Nengti said, “Yes. Give me a cigarette.”
Byomkesh handed him one. Lighting it, Nengti took two or three deep drags and said, “Last night, someone set fire to Hena’s room and burned it down.”
I exclaimed, “What! The house burned down?”
Nengti replied, “Not the house, only Hena’s room. The bed, bedding, table, wardrobe—nothing remains, everything has turned to ashes.”
Byomkesh remained silent for a while, then asked, “When did you all find out?”
Nengti said, “How would we know at night? We sleep upstairs. Rabivarma sleeps downstairs, but even he didn’t know anything. It was only discovered early this morning.”
“And then?”
“What else? The whole house is in an uproar. I slipped away to come and tell you.”
“Hm. Who could have set the fire—someone from the house, or an outsider?”
“How would I know? At night, all the doors and windows on the ground floor are kept shut.”
“When you saw it in the morning, were Hena’s room’s windows open?”
“The doors and windows are all burned to charcoal—there’s no way to tell if they were open or closed. But—” Nengti broke off.
Byomkesh asked, “But what?”
Nengti’s cigarette was half-smoked; carefully extinguishing the rest, he put it in his pocket and said, “There used to be a tin of petrol kept under the stairs. It’s empty now.”
“That means—” Byomkesh left his sentence unfinished, sinking into thought.
Nengti got up and said, “I’d better run. If Mashima finds out I’m not at home,
Byomkesh Samagra
There will be no escape.’
Byomkesh raised his head and said, ‘Sit down. I have a couple of questions for you.’
Reluctantly, Nengti sat and said, ‘What more do you want to ask? I’ve told you everything I know. Now it’s up to you to use your brains and figure out who committed the murder.’
Byomkesh said, ‘There’s still no proof that it was a murder. But let that be. Where were you at the time when Hena fell from the roof?’
Nengti replied, ‘I wasn’t in the house, I’d gone out for a smoke.’
‘How do you know that it was exactly when you went out for a smoke that Hena fell from the roof?’

‘Listen. Just before half past five, as I was leaving the house, I noticed Hena’s door was slightly ajar. I saw her sitting on the bed, knitting a woolen vest with a needle. When I came back half an hour later, the house was in an uproar—Hena’s body had just been found.’
‘Who found the body?’
‘Ravivarma.’
‘When you left, was there anyone else in the hall?’
‘Uday-da was there, no one else.’
‘When you came back after your smoke, was everyone in the house present?’
Nengti thought for a moment and said, ‘Everyone except Mesomoshai was present.’
Byomkesh was silent for a while, thinking, then said, ‘One more thing. Did Hena ever receive any letters?’
Nengti replied firmly, ‘No, she didn’t. Whenever letters arrive, morning or evening, I take them from the peon. Not a single letter has come for Hena till today.’
‘Did Hena have any contact with anyone outside?’
Nengti began to shake his head, then stopped, and looked at Byomkesh with furrowed brows.
Byomkesh said, ‘What is it?’
Nengti said, ‘I forgot to mention this, Byomkesh-da. Perhaps it seemed trivial, that’s why it slipped my mind—’
Byomkesh said, ‘Trivial or not, tell me.’

Nengti began slowly, thinking as he spoke, ‘About ten or twelve days after Hena arrived, this started happening. There isn’t much traffic on our street—hardly any cars or motors—quiet, upper-class para. One afternoon, a taxi drove slowly past our house, and inside, a man was playing a mouth organ. You know what a mouth organ is, right? Looks like a spectacle case, you rub it on your lips and it makes a loud, shrill sound—’
‘I know. Go on.’

‘The taxi went by, and two or three minutes later, it passed again from the opposite direction, the mouth organ still playing as it went by our house. Within ten or fifteen minutes of this, Hena locked her room and left. The first time, I didn’t realize the connection—’
‘Did you see the man playing the mouth organ?’
‘I did. He was wearing a coat and trousers.’
‘And then?’
‘Then, for ten or twelve days, nothing—Hena didn’t leave the house. One day, I was upstairs—’
Magna Mainak                                     771

I was standing by the window of the hall, gazing out onto the street, when I saw a taxi approaching. As it neared the house, a mouth-organ began to play from inside; but as soon as it passed the house, the music stopped. A little while later, the taxi returned, and once again, right in front of the house, it let out a peppy “peppo peppo” tune before driving off. I began to wonder, what’s going on—why play the mouth-organ right in front of our house? Just then, I saw Hena step out of the house and head in the same direction the taxi had gone. Suddenly, I understood—someone signals to Hena, and at once she goes out to meet them.
“When would Hena return?”
“She’d be back in about an hour.”
“Do you know where she went?”
“How would I know? Once, I tried following her. About a hundred yards from the house, the taxi was waiting by the roadside. Hena slipped into it, and the taxi drove away.”
“Hm. When was the last time Hena went out?”
“Ten or twelve days ago. —Well, Byomkesh-da, I’ll take my leave now, it’s gotten quite late. I’ll come again when I can.”
“All right, do come.”
After Nengti had left, Byomkesh sat in silence for a long while. At last, I broke the quiet and said, “What do you make of it?”

Byomkesh, distractedly lighting a cigarette, replied, “The business with the mouth-organ seems fishy, but one thing is clear—Hena was not entirely alone in Calcutta. Anyway, we can be certain about Hena’s death now; it wasn’t an accident, someone murdered her. Now the question is—who is Morgamainak?”
I said, “Surely the one who set the fire in the room.”

Byomkesh didn’t seem satisfied with that. Shaking his head, he said, “Could be, or maybe not. Think about it. Someone killed Hena, but we don’t know the motive. It could be sexual jealousy, or something else entirely. But the person who set the fire—their intention is clear: there was something dangerous in Hena’s room that they wanted to destroy. We searched the room thoroughly enough, but found nothing dangerous. If we searched again, maybe we’d find the deadly object! So, better to burn it to ashes.”
“What could this dangerous thing be?”
“Perhaps a piece of paper. If it were something bigger, we’d have found it.”
Suddenly, I remembered and said, “Byomkesh, that scrap of pink paper! What’s written on it?”
Byomkesh took the scrap out of the drawer and handed it to me. “A poem. Read it and see if it’s poetry at all.”
I read the poem—
The glimmer of your smile Stabbed my heart like a knife Your lips, so red, can punish The innocent, without cause.
I said, “Not bad—rather like some bizarre Sanskrit poetry. Who wrote it?”
Byomkesh said, “There’s only one poet in their household—Yugal.”
chapters.summary: Byomkesh and A.K. Ray investigate Hena's locked room, finding a poem that hints at her state of mind.

chapters.title: Ashes and Unanswered Questions
paragraphs: In the afternoon, A. K. Ray himself arrived, carrying a copy of the deposition. Today, his demeanor was entirely different. He joked with us, shared a few amusing stories, and proved that Byomkesh, instead of joining the police, was chasing wild buffaloes on an empty stomach. He partook of refreshments appropriate to the hour; then, at last, he turned to business. Handing the file of the deposition to Byomkesh, he said, “Here you go, have a read. But it won’t be of any use to you.”
Raising his brows, Byomkesh asked, “Why won’t it be of use?”
A. K. Ray replied, “According to the police department, Hena’s death is nothing but an accident. Further investigation is pointless.”
Byomkesh gazed at him for a moment, then said, “Have you heard about the fire?”
A. K. Ray answered, “I have. That was a coincidence. There’s no evidence that anyone set the fire deliberately.”
Byomkesh fixed him with a sharp look, then turned his gaze to the window.
At last, he said, “So, the task Santoshbabu gave me is finished. There’s no longer any need to protect his family’s interests.”

A. K. Ray laughed. “No. You can assure him the police won’t trouble his family any further. —By the way, when I heard about the fire, I went to Santoshbabu’s house. He was there. Yesterday, the photograph found in Hena’s drawer—I showed it to him. He said it was a picture of Hena’s mother.”
Byomkesh nodded. “What did the post-mortem reveal?”
A. K. Ray replied, “Nothing more than what one would expect in such a case. One of the ribs was broken and pierced the heart, causing instant death. No other complications.”
“Time of death?”
“Between five-thirty and six.”
Then, after a few more jokes, A. K. Ray clapped Byomkesh on the back and took his leave. Byomkesh sat in silence for a long while.
I asked, “Is A. K. Ray a very clever man?”
Byomkesh looked at me and said, “His intelligence is second to none.”
I said, “His only fault is being with the police.”
“Yes, his only fault is being with the police.” Byomkesh picked up the file of depositions.
Half an hour later, having finished reading, he handed the file to me and said, “There’s nothing special, but you can take a look. —I’ll step out for a bit.”
“Where are you going?”
“It’s been a while since I visited the shop. I’ll go see what Prabhat is up to.”
He left. I opened the file and began to read the depositions—

Rabindranath Barman. Age 39. One of Santosh Samaddar’s secretaries. Lives at Santoshbabu’s house. Salary: 350 rupees. Today is Saturday. After the master left for the office, I returned around half-past three...
Magmoinaak

I arrived. I did not notice where Hena was at that moment. She was probably in her own room. I rested in my room for a while. At half past four, the servant brought tea and snacks; I ate. Then, around five o’clock, I left the house. There were some things I needed to buy at the market—soap, toothpaste, shaving blade, aspirin, such things. When I stepped out, there was only one person in the hall—Uday. I did not speak to him; he was doing nothing, just pacing the room with his arms folded across his chest. Uday is a college student, but he comes and goes as he pleases, has no interest in his studies. I returned from the market at six o’clock. It was not yet dark. I left my purchases in my room and went to the rose garden on the east side. After strolling there for a while, I suddenly noticed something that looked like a human figure lying at the edge of the house. When I went closer, I saw—it was Hena. I shouted for help. The servants came running, as did Jugal and Uday—yes, both of them were at home. Together, we carried the body into the house, then called the police. No, the master was not at home. He is never home on Saturdays and Sundays. I do not know where he stays.

Jugalchandra Samaddar. Age 20. Son of Santosh Samaddar. I am a college student. There were no classes after two today, so I returned home at three. My room is on the second floor, above Rabibarma’s room. I came in, took a book, and lay down on my bed. I must have fallen asleep, because I woke up at exactly half past five. I got up quickly and went downstairs. No, there was no one in the hall. I walked in the rose garden for a while, then came back and went upstairs. Chingri brought me tea and snacks; I ate. Then I went to my room and sat down to study. I was not in the garden for long, fifteen or twenty minutes at most. Let’s say, from half past five to a quarter to six. No, I did not see Rabibarma in the garden. I did not see Hena’s body by the house. After six, I heard shouting downstairs and came down. By then, they were bringing Hena’s body into the house. I was not close to Hena; she was not close to anyone. She did not mix with anyone.

Udaychandra Samaddar. Age 20. Son of Santosh Samaddar. I did not go to college today. In the afternoon, I went to the club to play billiards. The club’s name is Great Eastern Sporting Club. I returned home at half past four. My room is on the second floor, above Hena’s room. I went to my room, changed clothes, and came down to the hall. Why did I come down? I am not obliged to explain. This is my house; I go wherever I please, whenever I please. Question: While you were in the hall, did you see anyone else there? Answer: Rabibarma was in his own room, sometimes coming into the hall. He left, I think, around five o’clock. Question: Anyone else?
Byomkesh Samagra
Answer: Nengti was prowling about restlessly, asked me for a cigarette, and then went outside.
Question: Where was Hena at that time? Answer: In her own room.
Question: While you were still in the hall, did Hena leave her room to go up to the roof? Answer: Yes.
Question: Was she carrying anything? Answer: She had a small mat. And a vanity bag.
Question: Did you speak to her? Answer: No comment.
Question: After Hena left, how long did you remain in the hall? Answer: Five minutes.
Question: Where did you go after that? Answer: To my own room.
Question: Were you close to Hena? Answer: No comment.

Mrs. Chameli Samaddar. Age: 44. Wife of Santosh Samaddar. Six months ago, Hena Mallik came to my house. I had no connection with her, never asked her to come upstairs. I can judge a person by their face—Hena was not a good girl. I do not know why my husband brought her into the house. I was annoyed. But a wife must follow her husband’s wishes—what could I do? There was no quarrel between my husband and me about Hena, not a word was exchanged.
Both my sons are good boys, of upright character. They had no dealings with Hena; my sons do not associate with such a flighty girl.

Today, between five and six o’clock, I braided Chingri’s hair—Chingri braided mine. After that, I went to the bathroom to bathe. I did not see Hena go up to the roof, nor did I hear any sound from above.
Shefalika, also known as Chingri. Age: 15. Fostered in Santoshbabu’s household. Our parents died two years ago. Since then, my brother and I have been living with aunt.

When Hena first came to this house, I liked her very much. I had never seen such a beautiful girl. Once I tried to be friendly, but she shut the door in my face. Since then, I never went near her again—Aunt forbade it. I heard her speak to Uncle a few times. She spoke nicely to him. Every ten or twelve days, she would dress up in fine clothes and go out. I don’t know where she went. She went alone, and would return after about an hour. Yes, every evening Hena would go up to the roof. I don’t know what she did there alone; perhaps she paced back and forth, or sat on a mat. Aunt believes Hena went up to the roof to secretly smoke cigarettes.
I do not go to school; Aunt never let me study at school. She says, in school and college...
M G MOINAK

Girls go astray if they study, they learn to smoke cigarettes. I learned household chores from Masima. This afternoon, Masima tied my hair, and I tied hers; then Masima went to the bathroom. I went to serve snacks to the brothers. Jugal-da was in his own room; after giving him his food, I went to Uday-da’s room. Uday-da was not there; I left his food on the table and came away. Then I too went to the bathroom to bathe. There are five bathrooms on the second floor. No, I did not know when Hena went up to the terrace. I did not hear any sound from above. After coming out of the bathroom, I heard shouting from downstairs, and learned that Hena had fallen from the terrace and died.

Nirmalchandra Dutta, alias Nengti. Age 17. Fostered in Santosh Babu’s household. Chingri is my sister. Since the death of our parents, we have been living with Masima. I do not study. Mesomoshai has said that when I turn eighteen, he will give me a job in his company. Hena was very beautiful, but terribly arrogant, she never spoke to me. In the house, she only spoke cheerfully with Mesomoshai, and exchanged a few words with Jugal-da and Uday-da. I know nothing about Hena. This evening, at half past five, I went out for a walk. At that time, Hena was in her own room. After six, when I returned, I heard she had fallen from the terrace and died. I know nothing more than this!

Having finished reading the statements, I smoked in silence for a while. It did not seem that any of these people had pushed Hena off the terrace. Uday, the boy, is a bit insolent, but that proves nothing. Did someone really throw Hena from the terrace? Perhaps the police’s assumption is correct, and Byomkesh is seeing tigers in every bush. But is the fire in the house also a coincidence? Nengti mentioned a man—every ten or twelve days, Hena would go to meet someone after hearing mouth-organ music. Who was this man? Was he the one who, for some unknown reason, murdered Hena? The terrace on Santosh Babu’s third floor is, by its very position, easily accessible to outsiders; anyone could climb up with the help of the ladder kept for the tenants. In other words, both the residents and outsiders had equal access to the terrace. When it was time for evening tea, Byomkesh returned. I asked, “What was your purpose in going to the shop?” He stirred his tea with a spoon and replied, “There was no particular purpose. My head felt stifled, so I went out for some fresh air. I ran into Bikash at the shop. He sometimes comes there to join Prabhat for adda.” Taking a sip of tea, he lit a cigarette and said, “It was good to meet Bikash. I’ve asked him to come tomorrow afternoon.” “Why do you need him?” “Whether I need him or not depends on Santosh Babu. I’ll see him tomorrow morning. If he dismisses me, then there’s nothing more to be done.” He alternated between tea and
Byomkesh concentrated on his cigarette. I asked a few more questions, receiving only vague, half-hearted replies. Knowing his temperament, I did not pursue any more fruitless inquiries.
The next day, at precisely nine o’clock, the two of us arrived at Santosh Babu’s office. On Clive Street stood the grand mercantile edifice, and on its second floor was Santosh Babu’s office.

Santosh Babu had just arrived. Upon hearing of our presence, he summoned us in. We entered his private chamber. On the table lay files of papers, two telephones; Santosh Babu sat alone at the desk. Today, he wore Western attire; his coat lay folded aside, and a costly silk tie adorned the front of his linen shirt.
Santosh Babu greeted us with a wave of his hand. As we seated ourselves beside the table, he raised his brows and asked Byomkesh, “Any news?”
Byomkesh replied, “You’ve probably heard—the police have concluded that Hena’s death was a complete accident.”
Santosh Babu started in surprise. “Is that so? I hadn’t heard.” Then, exhaling in relief, he said, “Well, that’s a weight off my mind. I’d been feeling uneasy.”
Byomkesh said, “But I am not yet free of doubt.”
Santosh Babu gazed at him with a hint of astonishment, then said, “Oh—you mean you believe Hena was murdered? Have you found any clues?”
Byomkesh replied, “First of all, the fire in the room does not seem natural to me.”
Santosh Babu stared into space and said slowly, “That’s true, a fire breaking out in the room isn’t exactly an accident. Anything else?”
Byomkesh then spoke of the mouth-organ player. Santosh Babu listened with deep attention, then said, “Hmm. But as far as I know, Hena had no acquaintances here.”
Byomkesh said, “He could be someone from Pakistan. Perhaps, for work, he came to Calcutta every ten or twelve days, and would meet Hena then.”

At that moment, the telephone rang. Santosh Babu picked up the receiver, responded with a couple of brief acknowledgments, then set the instrument down. Turning to Byomkesh, he said, “It’s possible—quite possible. So, what do you wish to do now?”
Byomkesh said, “If you permit, I would like to question everyone in the house.”

Santosh Babu was silent for a moment, then said, “Look, Byomkesh Babu, I engaged you to protect my family’s interests. But now that the police have declared it an accident, your responsibility is over. Of course, you will receive your fee—”
Byomkesh replied, “I am not eager for a fee, Mr. Samaddar, nor do I intend to extract a higher payment by doing more work. I only wish to uncover the truth.”
Santosh Babu said, with a trace of impatience, “Uncover the truth! Now that we’re free from police harassment, I have no interest in the mere discovery of truth—”
Again, the telephone rang. Santosh Babu had barely finished his conversation when the other phone began to ring. One after another, he finished speaking on both phones, then turned to us.
Magmo Mainak 777
He looked at us and smiled. Byomkesh stood up and said, “I won’t disturb you during your work hours. So—you have no interest?”
Santosh Babu replied, “No interest, but no objection either. You may question everyone in the house.”
“Thank you. Is Ravi Varma at the office?”
“No, he’s unwell, he didn’t come to the office today. He’s at home.”
“All right. Would you kindly inform the household that we are coming?”
“Certainly.” He picked up the telephone and began to dial the number. We took our leave.
We reached Santosh Babu’s house at around half past nine. As we entered through the gateway, Byomkesh said, “Come, let’s take a look at the garden first.”

We turned eastward. In the corner of the house, the two burnt, glassless windows of Hena’s room gaped open like wounds. The shadow of a silver pine fell across the rose garden, where countless white, crimson, and yellow blossoms bloomed. There was no scaffolding here; the lime-washed wall reflected the sunlight. Hena had died, fallen at the foot of this wall, but there was no trace left. The dust of this earth is marked by murder, yet it bears no sign.

At the back of the house, scaffolding had been erected. The masons had begun repairs; two laborers, iron buckets on their heads, climbed up and down the ladder attached to the scaffolding. The work progressed sluggishly.

We circled to the west side of the house. Here too, scaffolding clung to the wall, masons worked, laborers ascended and descended. Byomkesh looked up for a while, then, grasping the ladder, swiftly climbed up.
He peered once over the terrace from the third-floor landing, then came down again. I asked, excitement in my voice, “What is it? What did you see on the roof?”
He smiled and said, “There’s nothing worth seeing on the roof. The object of interest is over there.” He pointed outside.

Turning my head, I saw—the back gate. Byomkesh moved in that direction, and I followed. On this side of the garden grew mango, lychee, guava, and jamrul trees; we crossed the orchard and reached the outer wall of the house.

The back gate was narrow, its iron-barred door about five feet high. Though there was provision for a lock, the rusted condition suggested it had not been locked in many years. Beyond the gate ran a narrow lane. The servants used this path to come and go.
Byomkesh raised an eyebrow at me and said, “What do you make of it?”
I replied, “I gather that it’s possible to enter the garden unseen from outside, and from the garden, it wouldn’t be hard to climb the scaffolding to the roof.”
He clapped me on the back and said, “Bravo. —Come, let’s go inside the house now.”
In the hall, Nengti was standing outside Hena’s burnt room, gazing in that direction. Seeing us, he came forward. Byomkesh asked, “What were you looking at?”

Nengti replied, “Nothing. This morning, Masima came and sprinkled Ganga water in the room. The masons will start tomorrow. New doors and windows will be fitted, the plaster stripped and replaced. Luckily, the house is concrete throughout, otherwise the whole place would have burned to ashes. And us along with it.”
Byomkesh said, ‘Hmm. Where is everyone in the house?’
Nengti replied, ‘They’re all at home, Mesomoshai called. The brothers didn’t go to college. Should I call them?’
Byomkesh said, ‘No, I’ll go to each of their rooms myself. Where is Rabibarma?’
‘In his own room,’ Nengti said, pointing with his finger.
‘Alright. Then you go upstairs and let everyone know. I’ll just meet Rabibarma first.’

Nengti went up to the second floor, and we stood before Rabibarma’s door. The door was ajar; as soon as Byomkesh knocked, it opened. Rabibarma said, ‘Come in.’ He was wrapped in a grey dressing gown, his thin face looked even more gaunt—‘I’m not feeling well, so I didn’t go to the office,’ he said, trying to suppress a cough.
We entered the room. It was about the same size as Hena’s, with similar furnishings: a narrow bed, a table, a chair, a bookshelf. Rabibarma kept the room quite tidy.
Byomkesh observed Rabibarma intently for a moment, then asked, ‘Rabibabu, do you truly not know the phone number of Santoshbabu’s Nibrit Kunja?’
Rabibarma shook his head firmly. ‘No, sir, I really don’t. The master never told me, so I never tried to find out. I’m a salaried servant—why would I need to know?’
Byomkesh said, ‘That’s true. But you do know Sukumari’s home phone number, don’t you? Yet you didn’t inform her of Hena’s death?’
‘No, sir.’
‘Did you see anyone else making a phone call at that time?’
‘Sir, in all the commotion, I wasn’t watching everything. I think, after the police arrived, Nengti made a call.’
‘Nengti called me. Never mind that. Tell me, the night before last, when Hena’s room caught fire, you didn’t know anything about it?’
Rabibarma began to cough, then, restraining it, replied in a muffled voice, ‘No, sir, I didn’t know.’
‘Strange.’

‘It’s not strange, sir. I’d taken a sleeping pill before bed. Sometimes I have insomnia, stay awake all night. After what happened on Saturday, I thought I wouldn’t be able to sleep, so I took three aspirin tablets before going to bed. After that, I didn’t know anything about what happened at night.’

Byomkesh glanced around. There was a small bottle on the table; he picked it up—it was an aspirin bottle, nearly full. Setting it down, he picked up a heavy key ring. Many keys were strung together, weighty in the hand. Byomkesh asked, ‘What are these keys for?’
‘Office keys.’ Rabibarma took the bunch from Byomkesh’s hand and put it in his own pocket. ‘Most of the office drawers and cupboards—I keep the keys.’
Suddenly Byomkesh asked, ‘Rabibabu, where is your native place?’
Rabibarma, taken aback, replied, ‘Native place? In Comilla district.’
‘Did you know Hena from before?’
A shadow of suspicion flickered in Rabibarma’s slanted eyes; suppressing another cough, he said, ‘No, sir—’
Magna Moina K No.'
'You didn’t know her father, Kamal Mallik?'
'No, sir.'
'You know nothing about Hena’s death?'
Ravibarma hesitated a little, craned his neck to glance once toward the hall, then, lowering his voice, whispered, 'Don’t tell anyone, but I know something.'
'What do you know?'
'That day, in Hena’s room, I saw her knitting a woolen sweater. Do you know who it was for? For Uday.'
'For Uday! How did you know that?'
'One afternoon, I happened to see it. Uday brought a bundle of wool and gave it to Hena. She was making the sweater with that wool.'
'So Hena was close to Uday?'
Ravibarma fell silent, his eyes anxious. Byomkesh asked, 'And with Jugol?'
'I don’t know. Byomkesh-babu, please, let no one know I’ve told you anything. If Boudi finds out—'

Boudi, that is, Srimati Chameli. Everyone seemed to shrink in fear of her. I remembered, that night as we descended the stairs, I had heard her muffled voice: You will keep quiet, you will say nothing.
Byomkesh asked, 'You weren’t close to Hena yourself?'
Ravibarma started, 'With me!—I have avoided women all my life. I don’t have that affliction, Byomkesh-babu.'
'Good. Come, Ajit, let’s go upstairs.'

On the second floor, in front of Jugol’s open door, we stumbled upon a private scene. Jugol was seated at a table, pen in hand, notebook before him. Chingri stood behind his chair, arms draped around his neck, whispering something in his ear. At our appearance, she looked at us like a startled doe, then hurried past and vanished.
Jugol rose, a little embarrassed. 'Come in.'
Byomkesh smiled, 'I’ll let you go after just two or three questions. If you wish to go to college after that, you may.'

Jugol glanced at his watch. 'It’s late already, my classes were in the morning.' He moved away from the table and sat on the edge of the bed. 'What do you want to know?' There was a calm gentleness in his manner of speaking. The thunderstruck confusion of that night was gone.
Byomkesh took a slip of pink paper from his pocket and held it out to Jugol. 'Tell me, is this your handwriting?'

I saw Jugol’s handsome face slowly flush red. He took the slip, turning it over in his uncertain hands. Meanwhile, I picked up a notebook from the table and glanced through it. A book of poems, with several short quatrains written inside. All were poems of longing; one among them struck me as not at all bad—
Byomkesh Samagra
chapters.summary: A. K. Ray dismisses Hena's death as an accident, but Byomkesh questions the fire and a photograph, then questions Jugol about his handwriting.

chapters.title: Suspicions and Secret Motives
paragraphs: Rose, I held you close to my heart In return, you tore my chest with thorns My blood has flowed in torrents Paint your face with that crimson.
Here, it is not difficult to guess who the rose is!
At that moment, Jugal cleared his throat twice and said, “Yes, I wrote it.”
Byomkesh, his voice laden with sympathy, said, “You were in love with Hena.”
Jugal sat with his head bowed for a while. Then, raising his face, he said, “Love—who knows. As long as Hena was alive, I was intoxicated—afterwards, now—”
Byomkesh said cheerfully, “The intoxication is wearing off. Good, good. Was it you who threw the rose through the window?”
“Yes.”
“Hena wasn’t in the room then?”
“No.”
“Jugalbabu, that night your brother Udaybabu accused you of killing Hena. What was the reason for that accusation?”
Jugal replied slowly, “The reason—jealousy!”
Byomkesh said, “Then Udaybabu, too, was infatuated with Hena?”
“Yes.”
The same old tale of Nishumbha and Mohini. By some twist of fate, the ending of this story has turned out differently.
Byomkesh asked, “Between the two of you, whom did Hena like more?”
Jugal was silent for a moment, then said, “Now it seems Hena didn’t like either of us.”
“Other than you two brothers, was there anyone else who was drawn to Hena? For instance—Ravivarma?”
Jugal’s head jerked up. Disbelief flashed across his face.
He said, “Ravivarma! I don’t know, I can’t say.”
Uday was sitting in his own room, oiling the strings of his tennis racket. As we approached the doorway, he glared at us from beneath his thick brows and said harshly, “What do you want now?”
Byomkesh’s face grew stern. Raising his forefinger, he said, “You brought Hena wool to knit your sweater.”
Uday replied arrogantly, “Yes, I did. What does that prove?”
Byomkesh said, “It proves you were close to her. That day, when she went up to the roof, you followed her. There, you quarreled with her and pushed her off the roof.”

Uday stood stunned, his face turning pale. He stammered in fear, “No—no! I didn’t go to the roof. I followed Hena up the stairs, but before I reached the roof, Hena bolted the door. I—I didn’t push her—I loved her, she loved me too.”
Byomkesh said coldly, “Whatever else Hena may have felt, she did not love you. She was making you dance to her tune. Come, Ajit.”
We went and sat by the round table in the middle of the hall. Glancing back, I saw Uday stand dazed for a moment, then silently close the door to his room.
MAGMAINAKE

Turning around, I saw Sreemati Chameli emerging from a room in the back row. She seemed to have just bathed; droplets of water still trickled from the ends of her wet hair, the edge of her sari hastily thrown over her head, her eyes clouded with suspicious anxiety. We rose to our feet.
In a sharp but low voice, Sreemati Chameli said to Byomkesh, “What was Uday telling you?”
Byomkesh replied, “Nothing grave, don’t be alarmed. Please sit, there are a few things I’d like to ask you.”

Sreemati Chameli did not sit; perhaps she thought her body was still impure from the bath. In a tone of displeasure, she said, “You know best why you people are harassing us. What do you want to know?”
We remained standing as the questioning continued. Byomkesh asked, “Were you once involved with the revolutionaries?”
Sreemati Chameli replied, “Yes, I was.”
Question: You do not believe in non-violence?
Answer: No, I do not.
Question: At present, you and your husband are estranged?
Answer: Everyone knows that.
Question: What is the reason for this estrangement?
Answer: There are ample reasons.
Question: Do you suspect that Hena was your husband’s mistress?
Answer: Yes. My husband’s character is not good.
Byomkesh seemed momentarily taken aback by this fearless candor. At last, changing the subject, he asked, “Are Nengti and Chingri your own nephew and niece?”

Sreemati Chameli paused for a moment; the sharpness in her reply softened a little. She said, “No, their mother was my childhood friend, we had sworn sisterhood with Ganga water. There is no blood relation.”
