Question: Do they know?
Answer: No, I haven’t told them yet. I will, when the time comes.
With a smile, Byomkesh folded his hands in a namaskar and said, “Thank you. We won’t trouble you any further. We’ll take our leave.”
Sreemati Chameli fixed us with a piercing gaze as we descended to the lower floor.
Nengti accompanied us to the gate. Casting a mysterious glance at Byomkesh, he asked, “Did you understand anything?”
Byomkesh, a touch irritated, replied, “No. Did you?”
Nengti said, “Why should I need to understand? You are the satyanweshi, you will understand.”
On the footpath, Byomkesh checked his watch—“Half past ten. Come, there’s still time, let’s go pay a visit to Sreemati Sukumari.”
Sreemati Sukumari’s residence was in a genteel neighborhood of central Calcutta, not far from our own. Shops occupied the ground floor, while Sreemati Sukumari lived on the upper story.
As we climbed the stairs, the faint sound of mridangam and khanjani reached our ears, accompanied by a fluid, melting...
Byomkesh Samagra
A voice—“Radhe Shyam, Jai Radhe Shyam!”—Surely, this must be Sukumari the Vaishnavi, practicing her vocal exercises.

In answer to our knock, an elderly woman opened the door. She was round-faced, draped in a sari, steel-rimmed spectacles perched on her nose, her countenance seasoned by the experience of life. I surmised—Sukumari’s ‘Mashi’, and her business manager.

She seated us in a small room and went inside. We settled ourselves on the edge of a takht covered with a jute mat. There was no other furniture in the room, save for a single painting of Gaura-Nitai hanging on the wall.

The music from the inner room ceased. Mashi returned and led us inside. This was a much larger room, the floor carpeted. A thin, ascetic-looking Vaishnav sat cross-legged with a mridang in his lap, his posture reminiscent of a Jamini Roy painting. He looked at us with stern eyes, then rose and departed. Not far away, Sukumari sat with a khanjani in her hand. Bowing her head in greeting, she said in a melodious voice, “Please, come in.”

There are some people in whom the enchantment of youth lingers long after youth itself has passed. Sukumari was no less than thirty-seven or thirty-eight, yet what the English call ‘sex appeal’ still radiated from her in abundance; to put it plainly, the sight of her could stir unseemly thoughts in a man’s mind. Her tall, graceful figure was softened by a gentle, ingenuous face, her eyes slightly heavy-lidded. There was no trace of artifice in her, only a candid simplicity that seemed to weave a subtle web of enchantment around her. It was clear that she was not famed solely for her melodious voice; the unique blend of beauty, talent, and character that she embodied drew the admiration of the discerning. She seemed a timeless Vaishnavi, as if sprung from the poetic imagination of the great bards.
Byomkesh said, “Santosh Babu gave me your address, so I thought—”
Sukumari fixed her enchanting gaze on Byomkesh and replied, “He told me about you over the phone.” Not only was her singing voice sweet as honey, but her speaking voice too.
Byomkesh asked, “Then you’ve heard about Hena?”
Sukumari nodded a little sadly. “Yes.”
“Did you know beforehand that Santosh Babu had given shelter to a girl named Hena in his house?”
“Yes. I knew he had taken in his late friend’s orphaned daughter.”

Byomkesh, a little hesitant, said, “Look, I know about your long-standing closeness with Santosh Babu, so there’s no need for reserve with me. Tell me what happened that day—Saturday afternoon—right from the beginning.”

For a while, Sukumari stared at her toes, then said, “I have no hesitation, only pride. But he has his reputation to think of, so things must be kept hidden. You want to hear about that day—very well. We call that house the ‘chhoto bari’—the small house. That day, around two in the afternoon, after finishing my work here, I went to the small house. It had been closed for five days, so cleaning and dusting took me until half past three. Then he arrived.

“He changed out of his office clothes and bathed. He keeps five sets of clothes at the small house, and many English books. He went into his room and sat down to read, while I went to prepare the afternoon meal. He never eats food from the market.

“At six, he had his meal. Then he sat down to listen to music. There are no instruments for accompaniment in the small house; I only sing, keeping time with the khanjani. I remember, that day I sang three songs—one by Chandidas, one by Govindadas, and one by Jagadananda.”
M G MOY NAK 78-3

“It takes at least half an hour to sing a single pad. I had just finished Jagadananda’s ‘Manju Bikach Kusum-Punj’ when the telephone rang in the next room. Before I could get up, he went and answered it. Two minutes later, he returned and said, ‘I have to go at once—Hena has fallen from the roof and died.’ He left immediately, in the same attire he was wearing.”

When Sukumari fell silent, Byomkesh too remained quiet for a while. At last he asked, “You don’t know who made the telephone call?” Sukumari replied, “No. Afterwards, I inquired in this house, but no one here had made the call.” “Who in this house knows the phone number?” “Only Didimoni knows. No one else.” “Didimoni?” “My guardian, she looks after the household. Shall I call her?” “Please do.”

The woman I had thought of as ‘Mashi’ was in fact Didimoni; perhaps nowadays the title has changed. In answer to Byomkesh’s questions, she confirmed Sukumari’s words. She had not made the telephone call that day, and apart from herself and Sukumari, no one else in this house knew the phone number of the small house.

When Didimoni had left, Byomkesh made as if to rise and said, “Your morning has been spoiled.” Sukumari folded her hands and said, “Since you have graced my house, please listen to a song before you go. I have nothing else left.”

With only a khanjani in her hand and her clear voice, Sukumari sang. Vidyapati’s self-surrender—Madhav, I plead with you again and again. I had never heard her sing before, and as I listened, I was utterly entranced. The sweetness of her voice, the purity of her diction, the profound resonance of her feeling seemed to transport my mind to some rare, joy-laden realm of rasa. Until now, I had only seen her as a restless, bewitching figure; now I beheld her as a pure, serene, absorbed tapasvi.

It was past one by the time I returned home that day. After bathing and eating, I came into the outer room. Byomkesh was still getting ready when the telephone rang. I hurried to pick it up. At once, a torrent of words burst forth in a woman’s voice— “Hello, Byomkeshbabu, I am Chameli Samaddar. Listen, you suspect my sons have killed Hena. Wrong—wrong. My sons are not like their father, they are good boys of good character. Why would they kill Hena? I’m telling you, no one killed Hena, she fell from the roof herself. She was peering down, lost her balance.”

Having said this much, she paused to catch her breath. I said, rather awkwardly, “Look, I’m not Byomkesh, I’m Ajit. I’ll call Byomkesh for you.” There was a moment of startled silence, then with a sharp click, the call was cut off.

By then, Byomkesh had come and was standing there. I told him about Mrs. Chameli’s call. Lighting a cigarette and pacing, he said, “That lady’s temperament is highly nervous. She must have learned of the questions I asked her sons today, and it frightened her. The police—”
He hasn’t withdrawn his hand, otherwise he wouldn’t have called me.’
I said, ‘Byomkesh, today you examined everyone thoroughly. Have you managed to form any impression?’
He raised his hand and said, ‘Wait, let me think a bit more.’

In the afternoon, Bikash arrived, accompanied by a slender young man. There was no change in Bikash’s appearance or manner; pointing his finger at the youth, he said, ‘His name is Gopikesto, my apprentice. I’ve brought him along in case he’s needed, sir.’

There are some people whose faces are unforgettable after a single glance. Gopikesto was the exact opposite—so utterly featureless that even if you saw him a thousand times, you’d never remember him. Like a chameleon, he blended perfectly into his surroundings and seemed to vanish from sight.
Byomkesh inspected Gopikesto and said with a smile, ‘Very good, very good. Sit down, both of you. I’ll need you both. It would have been even better if we had two more.’
Bikash replied eagerly, ‘There are more, sir. I’m training a few boys in the art of tailing. If there’s work to be done following someone, they can handle it.’
Byomkesh said, ‘Yes, there will be tailing. We need to keep an eye on the movements of four people.’

‘All right, that’s settled. I’ll put Babui and Chiching on the job. They’re young, but they’re sharp.’ Bikash and Gopikesto sat down at the edge of the taktaposh. Bikash said, ‘Now tell us everything, sir.’

Byomkesh called for Putiram and ordered tea and snacks. Then he explained the situation to Bikash in broad strokes: surveillance was needed on four men—Santoshbabu, Ravi Verma, Jugal, and Uday. Where they went, whom they spoke to, whether they did anything out of the ordinary. There was no need to report to Byomkesh every day, but if anything seemed suspicious, he must be informed at once.

Having explained the task, Byomkesh said, ‘Begin the work from tomorrow. Today, I’ll point out the men to you. Santoshbabu should be returning from his office soon. Have some tea, then I’ll take you out to identify them.’ Bikash said, ‘There’s no need for you to come, sir. Just give us Santoshbabu’s address, we’ll identify everyone ourselves.’
Byomkesh gave him the address. Bikash asked, ‘Now tell me, sir, who is to tail whom? Whom should I follow? Santoshbabu?’
Byomkesh thought for a moment and said, ‘No, you’ll follow Ravi Verma. And Gopikesto will tail Santoshbabu. The other two can be handled as needed.’
‘That’s settled, sir.’
Finishing their refreshments quickly, Bikash and Gopikesto took their leave. I said, ‘So you suspect Santoshbabu as well?’
Byomkesh replied, ‘I suspect everyone. If you had been present there that day, I would have suspected you too.’
I asked, ‘Do you suspect Nengti?’
He said, ‘If Nengti hadn’t informed me, I would have suspected him as well.’
‘And Chingri?’
‘I do suspect Chingri. Perhaps you noticed, though he’s young, he—’
Mag Moinaak
He loved her. Hena stood before him as a rival, so he had a motive. And plenty of opportunity.’
‘Where’s the opportunity? If we are to believe Uday, Hena went up to the roof and locked the door behind her.’

‘Who knows if Chingri had already gone up to the roof and hidden himself? The same logic applies to Srimati Chameli as well. She couldn’t tolerate Hena; she believed her husband was having an illicit affair with Hena.’
Turning Byomkesh’s words over in my mind for a while, I said, ‘Byomkesh, tell me what you make of this case.’

Byomkesh replied, ‘I can say one thing with some uncertainty—this was no accident, but murder. The question now is, who committed the murder? Let’s consider the suspects one by one. First, Santoshbabu. He’s a big man, a renowned political leader. But he has a weakness. He took in the beautiful daughter of his deceased friend. This act of charity may not have been entirely selfless or benevolent. But why would he kill Hena? There’s no motive for murder, or if there is, we don’t know it.’
I said, ‘Isn’t it possible that Hena was blackmailing him over Sukumari?’

‘Hena is from Pakistan, she shouldn’t know anything about the Sukumari affair. Even if she did, why would Santoshbabu give her shelter in his own house? And what would he have to fear from blackmail? His wife knows his character is not good, his sons know he doesn’t come home on Saturdays and Sundays. Ravi Varma knows, Nengti knows, everyone in the house knows, so outsiders must know too. But no one dares say anything, no one can prove anything. Why would Santoshbabu be afraid of Hena?’
‘That’s true. Besides, he has an alibi.’

‘Not just his alibi, but Sukumari’s as well. The two of them are providing each other’s alibi. Sukumari can’t be ruled out as a suspect either, however little her opportunity, her motive is strong enough. She gets a thousand rupees a month from Santoshbabu, perhaps there’s some affection too. If she saw Hena as a rival, she had a motive to kill her.’
‘Do you really suspect Sukumari?’
‘It’s not a question of truth or falsehood, it’s a matter of accounting—one can’t leave out even a single coin.’
‘And then?’

‘Then Ravi Varma. He had plenty of opportunity, but the motive is problematic. The man’s nature is like a slippery fish—try to catch him and he slips away. I think Ravi Varma knew Hena from before. He felt both attraction and repulsion toward her. The attraction I can understand—Ravi Varma is unmarried, it’s no surprise he would be drawn to a beautiful girl like Hena. But what about the repulsion? Did Hena know some dangerous secret about him? Was it resentment because Hena did not encourage his advances? Is that why he wants to frame Uday?’
‘He wants to frame Uday?’
‘Uday bought Hena wool, Hena was knitting a sweater for him—he didn’t need to tell me that. It makes me think he wants to shift suspicion from himself onto Uday.’
‘Hmm. And then?’
‘Then Uday. Stubborn, hot-tempered boy, but deeply attracted to Hena.’
Byomkesh Samagra

It happened. Hena, perhaps, showed him a little more favor than the others; Uday thought Hena loved him. Then he learned that Jugol and Hena were exchanging poems, exchanging roses. On the rooftop, Uday quarreled with Hena about this, and in a fit of rage, he pushed Hena off the roof. Perhaps he had no intention of killing her—'
I said, 'And Jugol? What was his motive?'

He replied, 'The same motive—sexual jealousy. Jugol is a gentle, quiet poet, but who can say what kind of uncontrollable fire might have flared up within him? If he found out that Hena was knitting a woolen sweater for Uday—'
'But how did he get to the roof? Uday had followed Hena up the stairs.'

'Jugol had gone to the garden, picked a rose, and tossed it through the window onto Hena's table. After that, would it have been so difficult for him to climb up to the roof by the gardener's ladder?'
'No, not difficult. But did he kill her right after giving her a rose?'
'The rose might have been a ruse, an attempt to throw dust in the eyes of the police.'
'I see. Who else remains?'
'Mrs. Chameli and Chingri. Both had motives, both had equal opportunity. When Mrs. Chameli was in the bathroom, Chingri was alone; and when Chingri was in the bathroom, Mrs. Chameli was alone.'
I said, 'So where does that leave us? Who is the real culprit among these seven?'
He said, 'Not just seven—there is another, a dark horse, who used to signal Hena by playing the mouth-organ.'
Of course, I had forgotten about Banshibadan Banamali. I asked, 'Byomkesh, who is that man?'

Byomkesh, deep in thought, said, 'I can't say if he is Hindu or Muslim, but there is no doubt he is a Pakistani. Perhaps there was an affair between the two; the man used to bring Hena books from Pakistan. In matters of love, who can say what might happen? Perhaps love gradually turned to poison, Hena's heart began to lean towards Uday.'
'Why did the man come every ten or twelve days?'
'Perhaps he came by plane, perhaps he was an officer on a plane; every ten or twelve days he landed at Dum Dum, met Hena in secret. All this, of course, is conjecture.'
After a moment of silence, he suddenly got up and went into the next room. I heard him making a phone call. Two or three minutes later, when he returned, I asked, 'Whom did you call?'
He said, 'Nengti. I was checking whether the man with the flute had come after Hena's death. Nengti said, he hasn't.'
'Why might he not have come?'

'Perhaps he heard of Hena's death, perhaps he fell ill, perhaps he died. There could be so many reasons.' Suddenly, Byomkesh fixed his gaze on me, staring for a long time. I saw that though he was looking at me, he was not seeing me; with his mind's eye, he was witnessing something unimaginable. Then, in a low, restrained voice, he said, 'Ajit.'
I said, 'What is it?'
He said, 'Do you remember the day Hena died?'
'Why wouldn't I remember? It was just the day before yesterday!'
MAG MAINA K
“Yes, yes, you read the news to me that afternoon. A Pakistani plane was sabotaged and went down in the Bay of Bengal, remember? I told the story of Mount Mainak—”
“Of course I remember!”
“Can you find that day’s newspaper?”
“I can.”

The old newspapers were always stacked in one place; at the end of the month, Putiram would sell them off. I fetched that day’s paper and handed it to Byomkesh, who eagerly flipped through the pages, searching for the account of the air disaster.
I asked, “What are you looking at?”

Without lifting his gaze from the paper, he replied, “Dakota plane. A run from Singapore to Cairo. All the officers were Muslim, except for one English pilot. Among the passengers, there were people of every nationality—”
Slowly, Byomkesh folded the paper and sat gazing vacantly at the rafters above.

After that, the burst of activity that had seized us seemed to die away as suddenly as a gust of wind. For two days, there was no sign or sound. Only Bikash called once to say they were still on the hunt. Santoshbabu and Ravi Varma continued their routine—going to the office and returning home; Jugal and Uday went to college and came back; one afternoon, Uday had gone out to play hockey. There was nothing else of note.
On the third day—Thursday—life returned to us once more, as if a dying lamp had suddenly flared up again.
That morning, Nengti arrived. There was a hint of unease in his manner. Byomkesh handed him a cigarette and asked, “Any news?”
Nengti didn’t answer immediately. Lighting the cigarette, he squinted at Byomkesh, then said, “Byomkesh-da, have you put a spy on Uday-da?”
Byomkesh raised an eyebrow. “Who told you that?”
“Uday-da said so. He claims some scrawny kid is tailing him everywhere.”
“Is Udaydi very frightened?”
“Uday-da isn’t the sort to get scared. He’s strutting about as if it’s a badge of honor. But Masima is frightened.”
Byomkesh looked up sharply. “Is that so? But why is she afraid?”

Nengti shook his head. “I don’t know. Yesterday, Uday-da was boasting to Masima—‘You know, Ma, the police detectives are after me.’ Hearing that, Masima’s face went pale. She’s always been a restless soul, but since then she’s been even more agitated. This morning she told me, ‘Go fetch Byomkesh-babu, I want to speak with him.’”
“She wants to speak with me?”
“Yes. —Byomkesh-da, have you found any clues?”
Byomkesh paused for a moment, then said, “I have found something.”
Nengti’s eyes widened. “You have?”
“Perhaps I have, but it’s not the time to speak of it yet. Come, let’s hear what your Masima has to say. Get up, Ajit.”
When we arrived at Sambhashbabu’s house, we found the hall on the ground floor abuzz with noise and commotion.
Byomkesh Samagra

The game was in full swing. Chingri, wielding a palm-leaf fan, was chasing after Jugal, intent on striking him, while Uday, clutching Chingri’s long braid as though it were a horse’s rein, tried to rein her in, calling out, “Haat, horse—haat, haat!” Chingri protested, “Why did you undo my hair?” All three burst into peals of laughter, darting about the room, their faces alight with mischievous glee.

Our arrival brought their revelry to an abrupt halt. For a moment, the trio stood awkwardly, caught off guard; then, with a blush, Chingri fled up the stairs, while Jugal and Uday followed at a more measured pace.
Nengti showed us to our seats and went to inform Masima of our arrival. I whispered quietly to Byomkesh, “See how close they’ve become, like brothers?”
Byomkesh gave a faint, grave smile. “This is what youth is,” he replied.
Nengti soon returned and announced, “Masima is calling you upstairs.”

We ascended to the upper floor, but found the hall empty. Those who had just come up must have retreated to their respective rooms. Nengti knocked on the panel of a half-closed door. A voice called from within, “Come in.”
Nengti pushed open the door and ushered us inside.

The room was spacious for a bedroom; a double-bed occupied one side, but could not diminish the sense of space. It was here, perhaps, that Sreemati Chameli slept, with Chingri beside her. Besides the bed, there was a wardrobe, a clothes-stand, a dressing table, and two comfortable armchairs. On the wall hung a vivid painting of Ma Kali, her tongue lolling. Through two large windows, one could see a row of pines at the back of the house.

There were two women in the room. First, Sreemati Chameli: she had bathed and donned a silk sari, a rudraksha garland at her throat, a large vermilion mark like a silver coin on her brow, her face grave, her eyes burning with a strange, suppressed excitement. Second, Chingri. Her playful restlessness had vanished. She stood by the window, craning her neck, staring at us with wide, startled eyes.
Sreemati Chameli said, “Nengti, Chingri, go outside. I wish to speak to them alone.”

Chingri was reluctant to leave; she moved at a snail’s pace from the window to the door, but Nengti frowned deeply and signaled her with a nod. The two girls left the room, and Nengti pulled the door to.
Sreemati Chameli gestured to the chairs. “Please, sit down.” Her manner of speaking was clipped, as if she were weighing every word with utmost caution.
Byomkesh replied, “Please, you sit as well.”

There were only two chairs in the room; a third person would have to perch on the edge of the bed. Sreemati Chameli glanced at the bed, her lips curling slightly in distaste. “I won’t sit. My worship is not yet done. Please, you sit.”
As I took my seat, I mused: once, she had been a revolutionary, wielding firearms; surely, she had no such fastidiousness then. How circumstances change the mind.

Once we were seated, Sreemati Chameli began to speak, her words slow and deliberate, counting out each syllable. She spoke of ordinary household matters, none of which could possibly interest Byomkesh; it seemed she was afraid, and was circling around the real subject, delaying it with small talk.

After listening intently for a while, Byomkesh raised his head and said, “Please, do not be anxious. I am a friend of this family. Santoshbabu has entrusted me with the protection of everyone’s interests—”
...have done. If you know anything about Hena’s death, you can tell me openly.’
Shrimati Chameli hesitated for a moment, then regarded Byomkesh with a new, searching gaze and said, ‘You’re not with the police, are you?’
Byomkesh replied, ‘No, I have no connection with the police.’
‘But—but—you know the police have set detectives after my sons!’
I realized Shrimati Chameli did not know that the police had already withdrawn from this case. With her conversation with Santoshbabu at an end, who would have told her?
Byomkesh remained silent. Shrimati Chameli’s voice rose, sharp and indignant, ‘Is this not an injustice? My sons are innocent. Yet they must be shadowed by spies?’
Byomkesh answered in a calm tone, ‘Perhaps spies have been set on them precisely because people want to know if they are innocent.’
‘I have said a thousand times that my sons are innocent, yet they do not believe me!’

‘But how do you know they are innocent? Please don’t take offense—you are their mother, it is natural for you to believe in their innocence. But for outsiders, it is not so. In their eyes, everyone is equal.’
A shadow of inner speculation flickered in Shrimati Chameli’s eyes. She stepped forward and, in a hushed voice, said suddenly, ‘Byomkeshbabu, I know how Hena died. I saw it with my own eyes.’
Byomkesh started, his eyes widening. ‘You saw it with your own eyes?’

‘Yes.’ Shrimati Chameli spoke in a single breath, ‘That day, after Chingri went to the bathroom, I came outside and saw Hena heading up to the roof on the third floor. Everyone knows I cannot tolerate Hena, and Hena herself is afraid of me. I thought, if I seize this opportunity to go up to the roof and give her a piece of my mind, perhaps she will leave my house, and my sons will be safe.’
‘So you were anxious about your sons’ safety? Well, then what happened?’
chapters.summary: Jugal confesses to writing a poem and throwing a rose. Chameli claims she witnessed Hena's death.

chapters.title: Confessions and Revelations Unfold
paragraphs: ‘I too climbed the stairs to the third-floor roof. The moment she saw me, Hena panicked, ran toward the parapet, and crashed against it. Then, unable to regain her balance, she toppled over and fell down. Perhaps, seeing me, she was afraid I would harm her!’
Byomkesh gazed at her intently and asked, ‘Why did you never mention this before?’
Shrimati Chameli made a restless gesture with her mouth and said, ‘Would anyone have believed me if I had? On the contrary, they would have suspected that I pushed Hena over.’
Byomkesh bowed his head for a moment, then looked up again. ‘True enough. Tell me, when you went up to the roof by the stairs, did you see Uday?’
Shrimati Chameli replied, her voice tinged with unease, ‘No, Uday was not there.’
‘Did you see anyone else?’
‘No, no one.’
‘The stair door, the door to the roof—they were open, I suppose?’
‘Yes, they were open.’
‘When you saw Hena, what was she doing?’
‘She was standing in the middle of the roof.’
‘Was there anything in her hand?’
‘I didn’t notice.’
Byomkesh exhaled deeply and stood up. He said, “I suppose you have nothing more to say. Very well, then—we’ll take our leave. You may try telling the police your story.”
Sreemati Chameli stood there, rigid and unmoving, as we took our leave.
By the time we returned home, it was already afternoon.

The intricate fiction Sreemati Chameli had spun to save her sons had only left Byomkesh more bewildered and despondent. He stretched himself out on the taktaposh, and in a voice rough with agitation, said, “Nothing is happening—nothing at all. It’s all a sham, all deception. Everyone is trying to pull the wool over my eyes.”
I said, “But why are you so invested, Byomkesh? The police have given up, Santoshbabu has lost interest—so why are you wearing yourself out for nothing?”

Byomkesh replied, his voice weary, “Do you know what the trouble is? I am a satyanweshi—a seeker of truth. Until I know the real story, I cannot find peace. Damn it! If only I had another case at hand right now, perhaps I could forget—”
At that moment, the postman arrived at the front door.
An envelope, registered and insured. The sender’s name—Office of the Government of Orissa. My curiosity was piqued—what could this be? Byomkesh opened the envelope and took out a typewritten letter.
The Chief Secretary of the Government of Orissa had written—

Dear Sir, By order of the Honorable Chief Minister, I write this letter to you. The work you have previously done for the Central Government and the Bombay Government is well known to us. Recently, some mysterious incidents have begun to occur in the offices of the Orissa Government. Valuable and highly confidential documents have been disappearing from the department, but the culprit remains at large. In this matter, the Government of Orissa seeks your assistance. We would be obliged if you could come to Cuttack at once and take charge of the investigation. Any delay may result in loss to the state. We would appreciate it if you could inform us by telegram when you will arrive. Enclosed please find a cheque for Rs 500 towards your expenses. With thanks and regards, etc.
Byomkesh, his face alight with cheer, handed me the letter and the cheque. “It seems my reputation has now reached the corridors of government,” he said.
After reading the letter, I looked up to see him pacing, hands clasped behind his back. I asked, “So, you got what you wanted. Will you go?”
“It’s a matter of national interest. Of course I’ll go.”
“When will you leave?”
He paused in his pacing and said, “Ajit, finish your meal, deposit the cheque at the bank, and send a telegram to Cuttack. We are leaving at once.”
I asked, “And when, exactly, is ‘at once’?”
He smiled and replied, “Within today or tomorrow.”
It was almost dusk when Bikash arrived and said, “There’s news, sir.”
I had quite forgotten that Bikash, along with Gupikesto, Babui, and Chiching—four young men—worked as informants for Byomkesh. My mind had already raced ahead to Cuttack.
We three sat close together on the takhtposh, shoulders nearly touching. Bikash said, “That Chinaman is giving us a lot of trouble, sir.”
“Chinaman?”
“Yes, your Ravi Verma. His nose, mouth, eyes—just like a Chinaman’s. I’m sure he sneaks around eating cockroaches.”
“Not impossible. Go on, how is he troubling you?”
“I’ve been tailing the man for days, but not once does he stray from his routine! No, it’s always home to office, office to home. I was getting worn out, sir. Then today—”
“What happened today?”

“Usually he leaves the office at five, but today he left at half past four. Didn’t go home, got on a bus to Bowbazar. I got on too. The man’s conscience is clearly guilty, kept glancing back over his shoulder. I kept my head down. Near Sealdah, Ravi Verma suddenly hopped off the bus. I followed.

“You may have noticed there’s a hotel there—called the Indo-Pak Hotel. Three stories, but a bit dingy. Mostly people coming and going from Pakistan stay there. There’s a restaurant on the ground floor, chicken and mutton always cooking, and rooms to stay in upstairs. Ravi Verma slipped into the hotel.
“There was a racket in the restaurant, but Ravi Verma didn’t go that way. He crept up a dark staircase at the side.

“I followed. Where the stairs turn from the second to the third floor, there’s a narrow corridor like an alley, lined with doors on both sides. A smoky bulb hung overhead. From the bend in the stairs, I peeked and saw Ravi Verma unlocking a door at the far end with a key. But the door wouldn’t open. Then he picked another key from his bunch and tried again, but still the lock wouldn’t budge.

“At that moment, footsteps sounded above—two or three tenants were coming down the stairs. I pretended as if I lived on the second floor, took out my own keys, and stood in front of a door. Ravi Verma quickly stuffed his keys in his pocket and hurried down. I took a good look at his door and followed him.
“After that, Ravi Verma went straight home. I saw him safely back.”
Byomkesh’s eyes grew distant, lost in thought.
“Indo-Pak Hotel—Hena was from Pakistan—Ravi Verma—” Raising his gaze to Bikash, Byomkesh asked, “Did you notice the room number?”
Bikash replied, “Yes, sir; there was a brass number above the door—number 7.”
“Number 7!” Byomkesh’s eyes flashed with sudden light.
“Yes, sir, number 7.”

Byomkesh closed his eyes again, sinking into meditation. I too felt I had heard of this number seven somewhere, but for the life of me, I could not recall where. Bikash whispered to me, “Is there something special about number 7, sir?”

Byomkesh opened his eyes, placed a hand on Bikash’s shoulder, and said, “You’re the most useful man among us. But your work isn’t done yet. Go back to the Indo-Pak Hotel, keep watch in front of room number 7. We’ll be there within half an hour.”
“All right, sir.” Bikash departed.

Byomkesh went into the adjoining room and picked up the phone. Once the connection was established, he said, “Is that E.K. Ray? This is Byomkesh... I need a favor... You have Henna’s bunch of keys, don’t you?... Good, good. We’re coming to you right now, I need that bunch... I’ll explain in person... If you can come along with us, that would be best... Very well, we’re on our way.”
Replacing the receiver, he said, “Come, I think the mystery of Henna will be solved tonight.”
It was only then that I remembered—one of the keys on Henna’s bunch bore the number 7.

We bundled E.K. Ray into a taxi and arrived in front of the Indo-Pak Hotel at around eight o’clock. On the way, we spoke only once; E.K. Ray said, “But remember, I’m not the police now, just your friend.”
Byomkesh replied, “That’s fine.”
At the head of the staircase on the second floor, Bikash was leaning against the railing. On seeing us, he straightened up. Byomkesh quietly asked him, “Any news from room number seven?”
Bikash replied, “All’s well. No one else has come.”
“Do you know where the hotel manager stays?”
“In that room.” Bikash pointed to the room ahead.
Byomkesh turned his gaze to E.K. Ray; a silent exchange passed between their eyes. E.K. Ray nodded and knocked on the closed door of the manager’s room.
A middle-aged man opened the door. Behind him, we glimpsed a well-lit room furnished with a table and chairs. No one else was present, save for a bottle displayed on the table.
E.K. Ray asked, “Are you the hotel manager?”

The manager, his eyes bleary, surveyed E.K. Ray’s attire and replied, “Yes, sir, please come in.” As he bowed low in greeting, he nearly lost his balance and would have fallen had E.K. Ray not caught him. “I’m not here on police business,” E.K. Ray said. “I’ve come to have a word with you.”

A thick, syrupy laugh gurgled from the manager’s throat. E.K. Ray glanced back at Byomkesh, signaled with his eyes, then took Henna’s key ring from his pocket and handed it to him. After that, he entered the room and closed the door behind him. The three of us remained outside.
Byomkesh said, “Now for number seven.”

At the far end of the corridor was room number seven. In the dim glow of a flickering bulb, Byomkesh selected the right key from the ring and inserted it into the lock. Instantly, the lock clicked open. There could be no doubt now that this was the key to this room, and that Henna had frequented it.

The room was dark. As we stepped inside, it felt as if a black, savage beast lay in wait in the corner, ready to leap at our throats the moment we set foot within. Byomkesh said, “Wait, let me get a match.”
But Bikash had already entered, groped along the wall by the door, and pressed the switch. With a sudden flare, the room was flooded with light. We went in and closed the door behind us.

The stale, damp air of the closed room carried a musty odor. There was only one window, shut tight. The room was almost bare; against one wall lay a naked iron cot, and against another, a medium-sized Godrej steel almirah. Nothing else.
Byomkesh’s gaze immediately went to the steel almirah. From the key ring, he—
Magna Mainak 793
As soon as the key was turned in the lock, the almirah swung open. Bikash and I leaned over Byomkesh’s shoulder to peer inside.

There were three shelves in the almirah. The lower two were empty; on the top shelf rested a single book and, beside it, a file bound in rexine, shaped like a ledger. At the back, a dark object was barely visible. Byomkesh reached in and drew it out. It turned out to be a broken mouth-organ.

Byomkesh examined the mouth-organ, turning it over in his hands, then set it back in its place. Next, he picked up the book. It was a quarto-sized Bengali volume, bound in faded cloth, the title on the cover inscribed in imitation of Persian script—Rubaiyat-e-Omar Khayyam. Byomkesh flipped through the pages and stopped at the dedication. Written there: “To Srimati Meena ‘Matahari’, beloved.” The name of the giver, inscribed below, made me start. The name was intimately familiar.

Handing me the book, Byomkesh took up the rexine-bound file, opened it cautiously, then snapped it shut almost at once. From what little I glimpsed, it seemed to contain several letters written in Bengali script.
Byomkesh said, “Come, our work here is done.” I saw his eyes were gleaming with excitement. Once outside the room, he locked the door and said, “Now we can meet with the manager.”

In the manager’s room, the adda was in full swing; an empty bottle rolled lazily on the table. A.K. Ray sat with a half-filled glass in hand, while the manager, palms pressed together in supplication, was urging him, “Just one more sip, sir, only a sip. I swear on my own head!”
As we entered, Byomkesh and A.K. Ray exchanged glances; Byomkesh gave a slight nod. A.K. Ray made as if to rise and said, “Well then, for today—”
The manager, beaming, protested, “How can that be! The gentlemen have come; you can’t leave without a drink. I’ll open another bottle.”
He moved toward the almirah, but Byomkesh stopped him. “No, no, not today. Some other time. Tell me, Manager Babu, who stays in Room 7?”

“Room 7?” The manager squinted, thinking for a moment. “Oh, Room 7. A Pakistani gentleman has rented it. Quite an amusing fellow. Pays his rent every month, but in the whole month, he comes at most three days. Stays for half an hour, then leaves. Very amusing man.”
“Does anyone come with him?”
A sly glint flickered in the manager’s eyes. “A fairy comes with him.”
“What is the gentleman’s name?”
“Name!” The manager racked his brains. “I’ve forgotten the name. But no matter, it’s in the register.”
He opened a bound ledger and said, “Just as I thought, where could he go? Here it is—the gentleman’s name: Dhaka, Pakistan, Omar Shirazi.” He looked up, triumphant.
Byomkesh said, “Omar Shirazi. Thank you—thank you very much. We’ll take our leave now, but we’ll be back another day.”
Sidestepping the manager’s renewed offer to open another bottle, we descended the stairs. Byomkesh clapped Bikash on the back and said, “Your work here is done. Go home now. Come again soon.”
Byomkesh Samagra
Bikash departed. We hailed a taxi and set off towards the A.K. Ray police station, to see him home before returning to our own quarters.

On the way, A.K. Ray remarked, “The manager is the very embodiment of courtesy, but stubborn as a mule—he wouldn’t let me go without having a peg. He was angling to ply me with more. —Anyway, did you get your work done?”
Byomkesh handed him back the key and replied, “Yes. Aren’t you curious to know what I found?”
A.K. Ray shook his head firmly. “No.”
Back home, the first thing Byomkesh did was to carefully lock away Omar Khayyam’s poetry and the file of letters in a drawer. I asked, “I know Omar Khayyam, but who is this Omar Shirazi fellow?”
The old newspaper was still lying on the table; Byomkesh unfolded it and showed me. In the list of those killed in the Pakistani plane crash was the name—Omar Shirazi, navigator.
After dinner, Byomkesh sat down with the file of letters.
The next day, at nine in the morning, we arrived at Santosh Babu’s office.
Santosh Babu had just arrived and taken his seat. Seeing Byomkesh, he exclaimed in astonishment, “What’s this! You’re still here?”

Byomkesh regarded him steadily and said, “I had thought of setting a trap for you, but it seems there’s no need. Yes, I have received the invitation from the Orissa government, but I haven’t left yet. May I sit?” Without waiting for permission, he took a chair. I sat as well.
A careless word had slipped out. For a moment, Santosh Babu’s face flushed red. Then, regaining his composure, he said, “The Orissa government!”

A faint smile played on Byomkesh’s lips as he said, “At your recommendation, the Orissa government has summoned me; of course, they don’t know your true intentions. But let’s leave that aside. Santosh Babu, I have discovered who pushed Hena Mallik from the terrace.”

I was watching Santosh Babu closely and saw his face turn ashen, while his eyes grew sharp and venomous, like those of a serpent. In that instant, it became clear what a dangerous man he was—cornered, he was as perilous as a wildcat at bay. Clenching his teeth, he said, “Who pushed her?”
Byomkesh replied in an even tone, “You did.”
Santosh Babu’s voice sounded as if someone were choking him. “Can you prove it?”
Byomkesh shook his head calmly. “No. But it can be proved that you had a motive.”
“Is that so? Do you realize I could sue you for defamation and have you thrown in jail?”

“You don’t have the courage to bring a case against me, Santosh Babu. There’s no point in blustering. Listen, you engaged me to protect your family’s interests, and that is what I have done. For whatever reason, the police have closed the investigation into Hena’s death; I have no further duty in that matter. But everyone has the right to know the truth.”
Magna Mainak 795
“I know. I have learned the truth.”
Santoshbabu gazed at him for a while. It was impossible to decipher how many kinds of thoughts flashed like lightning through his eyes. At last he spoke, “What truth have you learned?”
Byomkesh said, “What you were searching for, but could not find—the very thing for which you set your house on fire—I have found it. A book—Rubaiyat-e-Omar Khayyam—and a few letters.”
The veins in Santoshbabu’s temples swelled. He looked at Byomkesh with helpless, venomous eyes and said, “What do you want? Money?”
Byomkesh replied in a dry voice, “You could not bribe me, Santoshbabu, not even with all the money you possess. You have betrayed, you have committed treason, and you must face punishment.”
Santoshbabu stared at him, speechless, the veins in his temples throbbing.

“You were in love with Meena, Henna’s mother. During the Partition, you used to go to Dhaka, meet Meena. You knew Meena was a spy for the opposing side, and yet you revealed your own party’s secrets to her. Not only did you confide in her, you wrote letters, disclosing every plan and counsel of your party. Because of that, we lost at every step, lost the land that was rightfully ours.

“Meena kept your letters. Then, suddenly, she died, and the letters came into her daughter Henna’s hands. Henna had an accomplice—Omar Shirazi. Together, they conspired, and then Henna came and pressed you, began to blackmail you.”
Santoshbabu’s eyes turned blood-red. Suddenly, he reached out his hand and cried, “I’ll give you a lakh of rupees—return those letters to me!”
Byomkesh stood up, and immediately Santoshbabu did the same, glaring with bloodshot, terrifying eyes. “You won’t?”
Byomkesh shook his head, then said quietly, “From tomorrow, a prominent daily newspaper will publish facsimiles of your letters, one by one. Be prepared.”
Santoshbabu, his eyes blazing, collapsed into his chair. Byomkesh signaled to me, and we made our way toward the door.
A voice called from behind, “Byomkeshbabu!”

We turned and stood before Santoshbabu. He sat with both elbows on the table, his face buried in his hands. After a minute, he lowered his hands; his face was expressionless. He said, “Will you give me one day? I have a speech at Park Circus Maath this evening at five—”

Byomkesh fixed him with a grave look and replied in a slow, deliberate voice, “You have one day. Tomorrow morning your letters will not appear in the newspaper. But let me warn you—hiring goons to have me killed will do you no good. You will never get hold of those letters. In due time, they will be published.”
“Thank you.”
All day, Byomkesh lay on the taktaposh, counting the rafters, silent. At four in the afternoon, when tea arrived, he sat up and drank his tea, then said, “Come, let’s go out.”
“Where are we going?”
Byomkesh Samagra

“To listen to Santosh Babu’s lecture.” Thus, we set out. It is only natural, I suppose, to feel curious about what sort of speech a man would give when the sword is hanging over his head. A stage had been erected on the Park Circus grounds, upon which sat a row of dignitaries, the Chief Secretary among them. Before them, a vast crowd had gathered. The meeting had been called to bring some grave political matter to the attention of the public. We took our place at the back of the crowd. First, the Prime Minister rose—he was the chairman. Standing before the microphone, he introduced the subject at hand. Then, one by one, the speakers took the stage. Each delivered impassioned speeches, laced with a touch of reasoned argument. Carried away by their eloquence, I found myself drifting on a tide of words. At last, Santosh Babu stepped up to the microphone. The resolute gravity on his face signaled the seriousness of the matter. He stood in silence for a moment, then began to speak, slowly and deliberately. The man had the gift of oratory. There was no bombast, no sentimentality—only an irresistible logic that drew the entire audience into his grasp. Gradually, the rhythm of his speech quickened, his voice resonating with a hidden passion, like the beat of a mridangam. And when, at the end of his address, he uttered “Bande Mataram” in a ringing voice, the crowd responded with a spontaneous chorus of victory cries. Finishing his speech, Santosh Babu returned to his seat. My gaze remained fixed on him; I saw him take a small tin from his pocket and put something in his mouth. I thought, perhaps, it was a penicillin tablet. Meanwhile, the Chief Secretary had come forward and begun his closing remarks. The audience was beginning to stir, preparing to leave, when suddenly a commotion broke out on the stage. Instantly, my eyes darted in that direction; I saw Santosh Babu slumped in his seat, those nearby leaning over him in alarm. The Prime Minister broke off his speech and rushed to his side. A wave of anxious murmurs swept through the crowd. Five minutes later, the Prime Minister returned to the microphone and, his voice heavy with emotion, announced, “With deepest sorrow, I must inform you that our dear friend, the nation’s beloved son, Santosh Samaddar, has left this world—” His voice broke as he continued. Byomkesh seized my arm and tugged, saying, “Come. The curtain has fallen on the fifth act.”

Once outside the park, Byomkesh lit a cigarette and said, “Let’s walk.” It was quite a distance, but neither of us felt like taking a tram or bus. I lit a cigarette as well and replied, “Let’s.” As we walked side by side, Byomkesh began to speak— “Santosh Babu was a man of talent, but he was not a man of character. There’s an English saying—‘A sailor has a wife in every port.’ Santosh Babu was much the same. His work took him to Madras, Bombay, Delhi—everywhere. I believe he had a sweetheart in every city. Even in old age, he never outgrew that affliction. “In Calcutta, he had Sukumari; in Dhaka, there was Meena. Meena was a Muslim by faith. In every country, in every civilized society, there exists a class of women who outwardly appear—”
Magnamainak 797

Refined and decorous, yet beneath the surface she ran the trade of a courtesan. In Western countries, such women are called—demi-mondaines. Meena was a demi-mondaine. Whether she had a husband, I do not know; perhaps there was someone of the shadowy, witness-Gopal sort, a certain Kamal Mallik. The name Kamal Mallik is Hindu, but if you say Kamal Mallik, it becomes a Muslim name. Hena Mallik is the same. The surname Mallik exists among Hindus, but in truth, it is a Muslim title.

You have seen Meena’s photograph—she was a woman of rare beauty. She had influence in the upper echelons of society. She had ensnared Santoshbabu in her web of enchantment; whenever he visited Dhaka, he would meet with Meena. Perhaps she sang him ghazals.

Then came Independence, and with it, the war of Partition. None can forget how brutal that conflict was. At this time, Santoshbabu was a prominent leader of our group. When envoys were needed between the two sides, Santoshbabu was appointed as our emissary. He began to travel frequently between Calcutta and Dhaka. Naturally, he continued to meet Meena.

Santoshbabu, then drowning in Meena’s love, began to divulge even the most confidential secrets of his party to her. Though Meena was a woman of pleasure, she still cared for her own side’s interests, and she passed those secrets to their proper destination. Consider the situation: a political war of intrigue was raging, we knew nothing of their secret intentions, while they knew all of ours. The outcome was inevitable.

Santoshbabu, in his besotted state, did not stop at revealing secrets verbally to Meena; when he was in Calcutta, he wrote her letters containing confidential information. I do not know the reason for this betrayal—perhaps personal jealousy against another national leader. But that he knowingly sent Meena these reports is beyond doubt. On the dedication page of a copy of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, he had written—Meena Mata Hari. He knew Meena was a spy for the opposing side.

In any case, the struggle of Partition ended one day. Several years passed. Meena had carefully preserved Santoshbabu’s letters; she had not destroyed them. What her intentions were, I cannot say—perhaps she thought if Santoshbabu ever tried to break free, the letters would prove useful. But suddenly, one day, Meena died. Perhaps it was an accident.

Meena had a daughter—Hena. When her mother died, she had come of age. Among her mother’s papers, she found Santoshbabu’s letters. Hena surely had a few suitors; her closest friend among them was Omar Shirazi. Shirazi worked for an airline company, a navigator on airplanes. He flew from country to country; his route stretched from Singapore to Cairo. Every ten or twelve days, his plane would land at Dum Dum.

Hena told Omar Shirazi about the letters, and together they decided to blackmail Santoshbabu. They came to Calcutta and made their intentions clear to him. Hena settled herself in his house. They had reasoned that Santoshbabu’s home was the safest place for Hena. Santoshbabu was caught in a snare. Even if he wished, he could not kill Hena—if he did, Omar Shirazi would expose his secrets. He began to pay the blackmail money.
Santoshbabu could not discover where Hena had hidden the incriminating letters, though he suspected she had concealed them in her own room in his house. But
Byomkesh Samagra

Since it was his own house, there was no convenience in searching it. Hena always stayed in her own room, only going up to the roof once in the evening to perform her namaz. Even then, she locked the door behind her.

“Omar Shirazi had rented a room in the Indo-Pak Hotel. All their evidence, their letters and documents, were hidden in that room. It seems there was an arrangement—Santoshbabu would give Hena money every week. I don’t know how much, but it could be found out by examining Santoshbabu’s bank records. In any case, Hena would wait for Shirazi with the money. At the appointed time, Shirazi would arrive and signal her by playing his mouth-organ. Then the two of them would go to the Indo-Pak Hotel. There, Hena would hand over the money to Shirazi, and Shirazi would leave for Pakistan with it. That, in short, was their method.”
I asked, “He took Indian currency?”
Byomkesh replied, “He took the money, or perhaps bought gold with it, or deposited it in some Calcutta bank. But I believe he simply took the money.”
“Go on.”

“Hena was not the orphaned daughter of Santoshbabu’s friend—she was bleeding him dry. Only one person suspected this. Rabivarma. He was Santoshbabu’s secretary, and a terribly cunning, slippery fellow. Whether he knew Hena beforehand is uncertain, but at some point, he followed her and discovered the Indo-Pak Hotel. He realized that Room 7 contained dangerous documents. He managed to procure a bunch of keys and tried to enter Room 7 at an opportune moment. But he couldn’t open the door. Most likely, his plan was to get hold of those documents and blackmail Santoshbabu himself. But his scheme failed. After Hena’s death, he tried once more. Bikash was on his tail and caught him in the act. If Bikash hadn’t seen him in front of Room 7 at the Indo-Pak Hotel, Santoshbabu would never have been caught.”
I said, “One thing. Isn’t it possible that Santoshbabu himself employed Rabivarma to recover those documents?”

Byomkesh replied, “No. If Santoshbabu were involved, he wouldn’t have acted like a petty thief. He’d have bribed the manager handsomely and got the job done. Anyway, let’s not get ahead of ourselves. Santoshbabu was caught in a vice, suffering for six months, with no end in sight. Then, something happened. One morning, opening the newspaper, Santoshbabu saw that a Pakistani plane had crashed into the sea. Among the dead was the name—Omar Shirazi.

“That was it. Santoshbabu saw his path to salvation. Hena didn’t read the newspaper, so she didn’t know yet; before she could find out, she had to be eliminated. He knew Hena went to the roof every evening for namaz. The house was under repair, so it was easy to climb up from outside. He made up his mind—he would kill Hena in such a way that it would look like an accident.
“It was a Saturday. In the afternoon, he went to Sukumari, consulted with her, and arranged his alibi. He had to plan everything meticulously.”
I said, “I didn’t realize Sukumari had lied so blatantly to us.”

Byomkesh replied, “Yes. Sukumari was deeply attached to Santoshbabu, or else she wouldn’t have entangled herself in a murder case for his sake. If anyone would mourn Santoshbabu’s death, it would be Sukumari.
“Santoshbabu entered his own house through the side gate, climbed up using the scaffolding—”
Magna Mainak

Henna was perhaps at that moment spreading a mat, preparing to face west and begin her prayers, when she saw Santoshbabu coming up. It did not take her long to understand his intention; frightened, she ran towards the eastern side of the roof to escape. But where could she go? As she neared the parapet, Santoshbabu rushed up from behind and shoved her—she fell from the roof to the ground below.

Santoshbabu unlocked the roof gate and, just as he had come, climbed down the ladder and left. The reason for unlocking the gate—so that even if someone suspected Henna’s death to be murder, it would remain uncertain from which direction the assailant had come up to the roof.
No one knew Santoshbabu had come to the house; having completed his grim task, he returned to Sukumari. But there was still one thing left to do.

The letters were surely in Henna’s room. The police hadn’t found them, but they might later. In the dead of night, when all were asleep, he quietly came down and searched Henna’s room. But he could not find the letters. Then, pouring petrol, he set the room ablaze. Immolation, with all the evidence.
Byomkesh fell silent. After a while, as we walked on in silence, I asked, “Who telephoned Santoshbabu?”

He replied, “No one. That was pure fabrication. Even after returning to his secret bower, Santoshbabu could not feel secure—what if Henna hadn’t died by chance? Besides, the letters had to be removed from Henna’s room. So he invented an anonymous informant; coached Sukumari about the telephone call, and returned home.”
“An extraordinary actor, this Santoshbabu.”
“Yes. An extraordinary speaker, an extraordinary actor—they are all of the same breed.”
“Tell me, Byomkesh, why did Santoshbabu appoint you to safeguard his family’s interests? Why didn’t he send you away right at the start?”

“Nengti had committed a misdeed and called me. If Santoshbabu had dismissed me, everyone would have suspected him. So, posing as a saint, he engaged me to protect his family’s interests. Later, of course, he tried to get rid of me, but by then, kamli nehi chhordti.”
“When did you first suspect him?”

“When I heard about the fire in the room, I realized it had been set to destroy some combustible material. What kind of combustible? Surely something not easily found. Naturally, documents came to mind. What sort of documents? The kind used for blackmail. So, was Henna blackmailing someone? Whom? Jugol and Uday could be ruled out; that left Ravivarma and Santoshbabu. But Ravivarma is a minor figure—one couldn’t extract much money by blackmailing him. On the other hand, Santoshbabu is wealthy, travels frequently to East Bengal, had allowed Henna to stay in his own house. Perhaps even the police’s indifference was due to his influence. He was also behind the attempt to send me away from Calcutta to Cuttack. So, in every way, he was the most suitable candidate. —By the way, tomorrow morning I must send a telegram to Cuttack, to find out if they still want me.”
“All right. What will you do with Santoshbabu’s letters?”
“I’ll burn them. Their purpose is served. Santoshbabu has atoned; there’s no profit in ruining his reputation. Let Magna Mainak remain submerged.”

When I returned home, I found Nengti sitting there. He had procured tea and cigarettes from Satyabati and was enjoying them in utter comfort. He had not yet heard the news of Santosh Babu’s death. At the sight of Byomkesh, he raised his eyebrows and exclaimed impatiently, “Well, have you still not caught Hena’s murderer?”
Byomkesh replied in an irritable tone, “I have. What are you doing here?”
Nengti, startled and incredulous, blurted out, “You have?”
Byomkesh said, “Yes. Or have you?”
Nengti stammered, “I—I knew from the very beginning.”
“From the very beginning! How did you know? Did you deduce it? Tell me the name of the killer, let’s hear it.”
Nengti replied in a faltering voice, “Mesomoshai.”
Byomkesh stared at him for a moment in astonished disbelief, then asked, “You know! How did you find out?”

Nengti spoke quickly, his voice dazed, “I saw it with my own eyes, Byomkesh-da. I was up in the pine tree behind the house, smoking a cigarette. Just then, Hena came onto the roof, about to lay down her mat and sit, when suddenly Mesomoshai climbed up from the west side by the water pipe. The moment Hena saw him, she ran towards the east, and he chased after her, pushed her, and threw her off the roof.”
Byomkesh fixed him with a hard gaze. “Why didn’t you say anything all this time?”

Nengti replied in a plaintive voice, “How could I, Byomkesh-da? He is our provider—how could I hand him over to the police? Still, I informed you, because I knew, if anyone could catch the culprit, it would be you.”
Byomkesh’s face softened. He placed a hand on Nengti’s shoulder and said, “Nengti, go home quickly. Santosh Babu has died.”
Dushtachakra
Dr. Suresh Rakshit said, “You simply must come, Byomkesh Babu. Given the patient’s condition, unless you go and reassure him, it will be difficult to save him.”

Dr. Suresh was around forty, a little thin and gaunt, his expensive and brand-new English suit somehow ill-suited to his frame. Yet his manner was brisk, his demeanor intelligent. This morning, he had come to see Byomkesh with a most unusual proposal.
It goes without saying that Byomkesh had no desire to visit a patient. With half-closed eyes, he looked at Dr. Rakshit and asked, “What is the illness?”

The doctor replied, “Paralysis—meaning, a stroke. The attack happened nearly three months ago. He survived the initial shock, but his blood pressure is dangerously high. His mind, however, remains clear. He sent me to you, hoping you might kindly come just once. If he finds some hope, perhaps he might survive.”
Byomkesh asked, “You are treating him?”

The doctor replied, “Yes, indeed. I am a tenant on the ground floor of his house, and also his personal physician. The man is immensely wealthy, a moneylender by trade. You may have heard the name Bishu Pal.”
Byomkesh said, “What name did you say—Shishupal?”

The doctor smiled. “Bishu Pal. Though some do call him Shishupal. I don’t know why. He is a usurer, certainly, but not a fiend for money. Especially these past three months, bedridden, he has become utterly helpless.”
Byomkesh said, “But what can I do? I am no doctor.”

The doctor said, “Let me tell you the real reason. Bishu Pal has a client named Abhay Ghoshal. The man is a scoundrel. In a time of trouble, he borrowed a large sum from Bishu Pal, and now refuses to repay it. Bishu Pal pressed him hard for the money, and in response, Abhay Ghoshal allegedly threatened him—said that if Bishu Pal demanded repayment, he would kill him. Immediately after, Bishu Pal suffered his stroke, and has been bedridden these three months. Of course, his life is not in danger, and with careful treatment, he may yet recover and walk again. But that is not the main issue. What matters is that he is now convinced Abhay Ghoshal will murder him—he believes that even if he forgives the debt, he will still be killed. You need not treat him; Bishu Pal simply wishes to unburden his heart to you. If you could offer him some advice, it might help.”

Byomkesh, a little absent-minded, said, “If someone is truly determined to play the role of Shishupal’s slayer, even Shiva himself could not prevent it. Still, since the gentleman so desires my company—”
chapters.summary: Chameli confesses to seeing Hena fall from the roof. Byomkesh learns of Bishu Pal's fear of Abhay Ghoshal.
